speechtext:
That the Order of the House of 22nd April, 1914, authorizing the refund of fees paid on Bill No. 150 (letter H-2 of the Senate), an Act

to incorporate the Prudential Life of Canada, be rescinded, and that that portion of the sixth report of the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce, reporting the preamble of the said Bill as not proven, be referred back to the said committee for further consideration.
Explain.

It is perhaps fair that in moving this motion I should mention some of the circumstances surrounding this legislation. The Prudential Life Assurance Company, a company incorporated under the laws of Manitoba, desires this legislation from this Parliament. It is opposed by the Prudential Life Insurance Company of America, a company that took its name from the British company of that name, and which has been doing business in the United States for about twenty-seven years. The American company was licensed by the Finance Department of the Dominion of Canada in 1909. The Canadian company was incorporated by Manitoba in 1902, but did not begin business until 1907. However, in the year 1907 the Canadian company started business in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, and further it extended its business to New Brunswick in the year 1910. The reason this legislation is desired is, that owing to the diversity of the provincial laws regarding insurance, the company finds that under its provincial charter it is practically prohibited from carrying on its business throughout Canada as a whole.
What is the abject of the legislation sought from this Parliament?	.

The legislation sought from this Parliament is to give Dominion incorporation to a company that hitherto has had only provincial incorporation, so that the company may be enabled to do its business throughout Canada rather than be restricted to certain of the provinces. The Bill introduced this year in the Senate was introduced in the House of Commons last year, and passed successfully through the committee stage and through the House, but it was stopped when it reached the Senate. This year, to overcome any fundamental objection, the promoters of the measure introduced it in the Senate, where it was successfully passed. It was then introduced in this House, and was referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce. The promoters of the Bill were somewhat surprised, when the measure came before the Banking and Commerce Committee, to find that for some inexplicable reason-or perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I should recast that sentence and say that for reasons they had not foreseen, a phalanx of members were gathered there, and for one cause or another opposed the legislation going through the Banking and Commerce Committee.
Various objections were offered to the Bill, and perhaps it is fair that I should summarize these. One was, that confusion would result from another company bearing the name 'Prudential' getting legislative sanction from this Parliament. May I direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to this difference between the name of the American company and the name of the Canadian company. As I have said, when this Canadian company was authorized by Manitoba to begin business, the name was the Prudential Life Insurance Company; the name of the American company being the Prudential Insurance Company of America. That there might be no confusion, the promoters of the Canadian legislation signified their intention to change the name, so that the new name would be ' The Prudential Life Company of Canada.' There would then be this fundamental difference between the two names: the American company would have as an affix the words ' of America ' while the Canadian company would have as an affix the words ' of Canada.' The American company would carry the word ' insurance ' and the Canadian company would be described as a ' life ' company.
Fox reasons that met the approval of the committee, however, the Bill did not yesterday successfully get through the Banking and Commerce Committee. Objection was further made that it would be an offence against international comity that a Canadian committee should give legislative sanction to a company whose name was so similar to that of an American company; that as the American company had first made application to the Dominion Parliament for authority to conduct its business in Canada, it would be improper that a provincial company should now be recognized. I might say, in passing, speaking of the possible confusion of names, that I find on looking up the record that we have in Canada doing business the Mutual Life Assurance Company of New York, and that we also have the Mutual Life Assurance Company of Canada. We have the Travellers Life Assurance 'Company of Canada and the Travellers Life Assurance Company of Hartford. That legislation was piloted

through this Parliament by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). We have the Phoenix Assurance Company of London and the Phoenix Assurance Company of Hartford. When application was made by the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada to the English authorities to carry on business in England, they consented, although there was a British company carrying on business under the name of the Sun Life Assurance 'Company, to let the Canadian company do business in England if the words 'of Canada' were added to their name. Therefore the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada is doing business in England to-day.
Objection was also raised that the American company was the big company and the Canadian company was the little company, and that the big company should have the advantage and the little company procure another name. That hardly seems to be fair. The Canadian company had the western sphere of business entirely to itself from 1907 to 1909. The American com. pany then entered the field of operation, and they now say: Although you came first and had provincial incorporation; yet, because we were first in Dominion license, you should be stopped from extending your business. The name 'Prudential' to the small company in the West certainly means more to it than the name 'Prudential' to the American company, with its extensive ramifications and business connections. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It seems to me that the hon. member is extending the discussion beyond reasonable grounds upon a motion to refer a Bill back to the committee.

I have not the slightest
intention of trespassing upon the patience of the House; but if any other method can be suggested to me than that which I am at present adopting, I shall be very pleased to carry out the suggestion.
Are any new facts to be presented to the committee for consideration?

The facts as they were laid before the committee yesterday I think
;Mr. Nickle.]
cannot be amplified if the Bill goes back to the committee; but the legislation is of such an important character to the company involved and the throwing out of a Bill simply for the preamble not being proven on the ground that the name is not satisfactory is such an unusual proceeding that I think the Bill should be referred back to the committee for further consideration in the hope that a favourable decision may be reached. Last year, without a murmur, the House of Commons passed this legislation and the Senate killed it. This year the promoters introduced the Bill in the Senate, believing that once it passed the Senate it would safely pass this House. Suddenly without a word of warning, the Bill is stopped by the same committee and the same House of Commons that last year allowed it to pass without a murmur.
Are there any provisions outside of the name which the company believe to be necessary for them to carry on their business?
The only provision, I understand, is the power to increase the capital.

The motion made by my
hon. friend from Kingston to refer this Bill back to the Banking and Commerce Committee is of a somewhat unusual character and one not usually pursued in this House. The House having committed a Bill to one of its committees and that committee, as my horn, friend has stated, with .a phalanx congregated there, that is, with an unusual number of members, having deliberated on the Bill and having reported, it would be a most unusual practice for the House, without a single reason being shown beyond the charge made by my hon. friend that the committee has decided wrongly, to order the recommittal of the Bill to the committee. I entirely .agree with your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that it is not proper now to go into details of the case. The Banking and Commerce Committee was represented on that occasion by the largest number of members it has had this session; and during the greater part, if not the whole, of two hours, this question was debated pro and con. The hon. Minister of Finance was present and gave his advice to the committee; my hon. friend himself and hie cohorts and his phalanx of members gave their views, and the judgment of the committee was unfavourable to my hon. friend. Under such circumstances, it would be con-

trary to the usual practice of this House and a slight upon the dignity of the Banking and Commerce Committee that this Bill should be relegated again to that committee for its consideration, without its being shown that there was a mistrial, that there was a paucity of members; that there were points which ware ill-considered or not considered. During the ten years that I have been in the House I remember only one case where a Bill was so dealt with, and that was a case where it was alleged-my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will bear me out-that there was such a small representation upon the committee and that there were certain facts not considered by the committee that it was open to the House, in the exercise of its discretion and in the fullness of its power, to relegate that Bill to the committee, which it did. Therefore I consider it would not be an exercise of the judicial or proper discretion of the House to treat the Banking and Commerce Committee in such a. way in this case. That committee having digested and disposed of and decided the whole question, it ought not to be again burdened with the consideration of the matter. Therefore I foor my part shall strongly oppose and, if necessary, vote against the motion of my hon. friend.

Possibly the fact that
in *the previous session of Parliament I had charge of the Bill now under consideration would justify a word or two upon my part. It may be that the ruling is correct; I question it not, that the merits of the Bill are not under review at the present time, and it may be that jthe hon. member for West Algoma is within his rights in saying that some special consideration should in the ordinary course be preser.it in the mind of the House before it would be justified in referring the Bill back to the committee. In my experience in the House, though, I have never been able to detect any rule that the House has come fto in the way of determining what these considerations shall be or how compelling they shall be before a Bill be committed back. Every Bill is treated, and I think should be treated, and every Bill for reference back should be treated, strictly on its own merits and on the merits of whatever considerations may be brought before the House in regard to it. It cannot be argued-and I think the only deduction from the reasoning of the hon.
member for Algoma is thait it must be argued-that as soon as a Bill passes the committee the House is entirely robbed of its deliberative capacity on the merits of the Bill itself. Or, puitting it another way, as soon as the Bill is thrown out by committee, if the hon. member for Algoma is correct, then the House is robbed of its power to deliberate on the meri'ts of that Bill.
I did not suggest that.

I can find no other deduction from my hon. friend's reasoning.
If his reasoning is correct, that condition will at all times prevail unless fthere happens not to be many members of the committee present. That, however, would not be a cause better than any other, because the committee itself should be the judge of whether or not its numbers are sufficient to enable it finally to pass upon the merits of the Bill. There are, though, especial considerations in the present case, and I think the important one is this:	the
Bill has already passed committee and passed this House, and the judgment of this same House has been reversed by committee. Is not that a material consideration? The Bill has passed this House in respect of *the clause which was a stumbling block to the present committee. I understand that it was stated when this Bill was before committee yesterday that the matter of name was not under review, that the name was not. objected to tvhen the Bill was before the committee a year ago. I had charge of the Bill at that time and I remember quite well that objection was raised to the name.
I do not know whether it was pressed very strongly in committee; if.it was not it was because the objection at that time appeared, I must say, more or less trivial; blit objection to the name was pressed by some one and the committee in its wisdom decided that the objection was not tenable and that the Canadian company had prior rights to the name. That judgment of last session was under review in this House; was favourably passed upon by this House and the committee now step in, rebuke the judgment of the House of last session and throw out the Bill. I am not arguing that the committee had not the right to do so; I am not saying that the committe was estopped from deliberating on the merits of the name merely because the same House of Commons had approved it, but I do say this: that the fact that the committe did so in

contradistinction to its own action a year ago and in opposition to the judgment of this House a year ago, is an especial and a material consideration that should weigh with this House in discussing whether or nod. the Bill should go back. I do not argue that there were not sufficient members present at the meeting of the committee. I myself came in only a short time before the vote was taken, in time, however, to hear the arguments raised against it by the hon. member for West Algoma. As a consequence, I do not know what degree of discussion did take place, but I was more or less conversant with the subject before I came in. However, there were sufficient numbers present at the committee, no doubt and I do say that the merits of the case itself are such that a very brief review of them would convince the House, were I permitted to give them, that the position taken by the committee is indefensible and that the committee offers a very serious precedent for this House to adopt if that decision is not to go back for review.

Supposing the Bill to be recommitted and reconsidered by the committee and that there be a much smaller phalanx of members present, what would my hon. friend say then as to the reason for its being recommitted?

I would say that those who had opposed the Bill had seen the error of their ways and had stayed away. After the Bill has received the notice that it does receive and goes back to the committee, there is ample notice to all members of the committee and there is nothing to hinder their being present. I must say that those interested in the passing of the Bill will welcome all who may come to that committee, be they opposed or be they not, and welcome a fair consideration of the claims of this measure on its own merits.
Would my hon. friend be satisfied if an adverse judgment were then given, and, if so, why is he not satisfied now?

When the adverse judgment comes I will give my decision upon it. I do not know what will produce it; it may be that there will then be special considerations, but I will say this: if my good friend the hon. member for West Peterborough will disarm himself of all prejudices that may now be in his mind and will address himself to this question with all the intelligence that he can command, I think I will be satisfied with his judgment 
on the merits of this Bill. If the Chair rules that I am forbidden to discuss the right of this Canadian company to retain the name under which it has been operating through six provinces of the Dominion and which it is now proposed to rob it of, I criticise it not; I bow to it, but I ask that it prevail throughout this discussion.

Before the
motion is put, I rise merely to say that I, as a member of that committee, voted in opposition to this measure, and I resent strongly the insinuation of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Niokle) that the members who voted in opposition to it were influenced in any way, or that they were asked to come to the meeting of the committee. So far as I am concerned, I wish to state emphatically that I was not asked to come to the committee and vote; I felt myself perfectly free to act as I did. While on my feet I may say also that I strongly resent a similar assertion made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) in the committee. I am surprised that hon. gentlemen should make such statements, because they include members of the committee who, I believe, went there for the purpose of conscientiously carrying out their convictions.
Motion agreed to.

On the Orders of the Day being called:

I want to call the attention of the Government to a very glaring and inexcusable error to be found in a map published by the Department of the Interior showing the number of chartered banks in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. In this map, Lawrence-town is represented as being east of the city of Halifax, and in Halifax county. Lawrencetown is in Annapolis county.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend is giving us an example of a little knowledge being

a dangerous thing. There is a Lawrence-town east of Halifax in Halifax county, as well as a town of the same name in Annapolis county.

But the one in Halifax county is not a banking town so far as I am aware. This map was sent to me by the manager of a prominent bank in eastern Canada. In calling attention to this error he said that the Lawrencetown where the bank is located is in Annapolis county, and not in Halifax county as indicated by the map.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is quite correct in that.

The map is to that extent inaccurate. I wish to call the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the error, as the maps are being distributed all over the country, I myself having received one. Lawrencetown in Annapolis county is quite an important place, but I never heard of the one in Halifax county.

On the Orders of the Day being called:

I desire to ask the acting
Minister of Railways and Canals, when he expects that work will be resumed on the St. Peter's canal. I understand that owing to a change of plan the contractor has been obliged to discontinue work for some time. In the present condition of unemployment throughout the country I am bound to say that it is a matter of supreme urgency that the work be resumed as speedily as possible.

Work on the St. Peter's canal ceased during the winter, as is usual, on account of the cold weather. During the winter borings were taken for the proposed lock, but the material turned out to be different from what was expected and the chief engineer is now considering the advisability of having the lock in another place. If that plan is adopted it may mean the closing of the canal for one season. I discussed the matter with the chief engineer this morning with a view to arriving at a conclusion on that point, so that work might be started at the earliest possible moment.

On motion of Hon. W. T. White, the House went into Committee on Bill No. 70, respecting Trust Companies, Mr. Blondin in the Chait.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) usually desires to know what changes, if any, have been made by the committee, and I shall be very glad to give him that information now. The committee gave this Bill very careful and thorough consideration, and made a number of minor changes. Some valuable suggestions made by members of the committee have been incorporated in the Bill. It will be sufficient for the present to mention that amendments have been made as to the following matters: Qualifications of directors, the quorum of directors' meetings, the forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls, the liability of shareholders to creditors, the liability of directors, 'loans to directors, and the investment of the company's own funds. The last-mentioned amendment is the principal change made by the committee. Under the draft Bill, the trust company was permitted to invest 40 per cent of its paid-up capital in office premises. That provision was changed by the committee so that 35 per cent of the paid-up capital and reserve may now be

so invested. Under the provisions of the draft Bill, 25 per cent of the capital of the [DOT]company might be invested in stocks of banks and incorporated companies. That was amended by the committee so that not more than 20 per cent of the stock of any bank and of the stocks and securities of any incorporated company may be taken by way of investment, the total not to exceed 25 per cent of the paid-up capital and reserve. This section is made retroactive after January 1, 1917, so that the trust companies incorporated hitherto will have between now and that date to arrange their investments so as to comply strictly with the provisions of the new Act.
When I was dealing with the Bill on the second, reading, my right hon. friend referred to the very wide powers which in the past had been granted to trust companies incorporated by letters patent from the Department of the Secretary of State, and asked if we would inquire as to how many of' these companies had organized with a view to seeing whether the powers of those companies which had not organized 'should be cut down so as to comply with the provisions of the new Bill. We made that inquiry through the office of the Secretary of State. We found that most of the companies had organized and were carrying on business at the present time. A few of the comparfies have not organized. The changes which have been made by the committee in section 66, which deals with the investment powers of the trust companies incorporated under this Act, together with the retroactive provision, effectually clip the powers of any of the companies which have not yet organized, and which have powers of investment wider than I think this House would deem it w-ise that trust companies should have. So I think the point which my right hon. triend had in mind has been met by the committee.
On section 4-Incorporation and organization :

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is aware, there is concurrent jurisdiction in the matter of incorporating trust companies. The Dominion of Canada has jurisdiction, and each province has jurisdiction, so that the Dominion could not, as a matter of right, interfere with the legislation of any province. The point was raised, I think, upon the occasion of the second reading of the Bill, and I stated that I had received communications from the attorneys general of, I think, two or more provinces asking in a general way what legislation we proposed to introduce. They evidently desired to have it before them in connection with some similar legislation which they had in mind for their respective provinces. We are sending copies of this Bill to the several attorneys general, but beyond that I think we have not any power whatever to interfere with their discretion in the matter of provincial legislation. The only thing that could be done would be by way of suggestion. In sending a Bill with a covering letter >ve

might possibly be able to do that, but of course anything like interference might be misunderstood and even resented.

There is
another way of determining the respective powers of the Dominion and of the provinces to incorporate companies. The late Government had this matter referred to the courts. I do not know in what position the matter stands to-day; (but we shall never have complete satisfaction upon this point, but shall always have clashing of interests and possible complications, until we have, whether by legislation or by judicial determination, complete knowledge as to the power of the provinces to incorporate companies. Take the case we have had before us to-day of a company which has been incorporated in Manitoba. It comes to the Parliament of Canada to have its powers enlarged, and very properly so I believe. That company recognizes that there is more security in a Dominion charter than in a provincial charter. If a company wishes to do business not only in a province but beyond it, according to my judgment, it should have a Dominion charter. We have allowed the provinces to give charters to companies, and many of these companies have obtained powers just as extensive as those obtainable from the Dominion. I would like to know from mv hon. friend in what stage the lawsuit is between the provincial governments and the Dominion Government as to the power to incorporate companies. Has the matter been prosecuted or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My recollection is
that the Supreme Court gave judgment in the matter, and that the case is standing for appeal to the Privy Council. I did not suppose that the Dominion or the provinces would be content with the decision of the Supreme Court, although that body is entitled to our fullest respect. I am afraid that I shall not be able to make a statement as to this matter without some notice.

Perhaps the
hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) can tell us in what position the litigation is. There has been a judgment of the Supreme Court, as I understand, affirming the right of the Dominion against the provinces. Am I right in that?

I regret to say that I
cannot give my right hon. friend any information. The matter has not come in any way whatever under my cognizance since I have been in office.

I am afraid that my hon. friend has not been ve'ry diligent in getting information in reference to this matter and that this remark applies not only to himself but to the whole Government. They have not been diligent in getting this matter settled in one way or another. I know that there is a conflict of opinion between the provinces and the Dominion and that the provinces hold very strongly to the view that they have the power to incorporate companies. The Dominion, I believe, has not been as diligent as it might have been in order to have this question decided. The only way to secure a decision is by a reference to the Judicial Committee of the Privy . Council, and if the hon. Solicitor General has not the information, I think he should exert himself to secure a final determination of the question.

I am quite aware that the matter has been under review judicially, and at the same time I know of many similar questions between the provinces and the Dominion that are under review, some of which, to a degree, and some altogether, are under my own charge. But this is not one of them. That does not say, however, that some other member of the Government may not have had it in his charge.

My hon. friend is young in years and young in harness. He has an excellent opportunity of immortalizing himself by having this matter decided once for all.

On section 34-share warrants:

I wish my
hon. friend would give us some explanation of share warrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Not the holder, but
is entitled to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I was using the word ' holder ' synonymously with ' owner.' A bearer share-warrant is a certificate that the bearer is entitled to so many shares, or is the owner of so many shares, and is entitled to receive the dividends thereon when declared. The bearer share-warrant is 
negotiable; it passes from hand to hand like a bond payable to bearer. For example, if my right hon. friend were the holder of ten shares under a bearer share-warrant and desired to sell them to another party, he could pass on his title by merely delivering the bearer share-warrant to the purchaser. It is important, of course, that the company should have a record, and a careful record, of all outstanding share-warrants that may be issued. The holder of an ordinary certificate or scrip certificate, for so many shares in a company, delivers up his certificate and makes application for the issue to him of a share-warrant representing the same number of shares. The company after cancelling the stock certificate, or certificates, delivers to him the share-warrant. It then has no record of the name of its shareholder, and the share-warrant passes from hand to hand. There has been a great demand in this country for share-warrant provisions in special acts and in general companies acts, in order to meet the requirements of the European investor, who otherwise would be obliged to send a power of attorney or a scrip certificate across the ocean, and make the transfer to the name of the party to whom he sold. Personally, I see very little reason why the provision as to share-warrants should find its way into an Act incorporating trust companies, but there have been trust companies incorporated with the power to issue share-warrants, on the ground that they derive certain of their capital from the continent of Europe, and so I thought it better, because the matter is certain to arise again, to confer that power upon the companies incorporated under this Act. It is open to the directors or the shareholders, by by-law, to adopt a different course and to provide that share-warrants shall not be issued. If the shareholders adopt a bylaw providing that share-warrants may be issued, I personally do not see that any harm can come to the public. My assistant deputy minister calls my attention to the fact that the share must be fully paid before a share-warrant is issued.

I have very strong
prejudice against this provision in an Act of this kind, and especially because of the secrecy it involves. I believe that the shareholders of any incorporated company in Canada should be open to the full light of day, so that every one who cares to know, or who is entitled to know, may know the personnel of those who constitute a company. If I am a shareholder in a company,

under this provision, I could go to the company, hand over my certificate for 100 shares say, and receive a share-warrant in lieu thereof. My name is then blotted out of the register of that company as a shareholder. The shares thus surrendered are suspended, and remain so as long as the share-warrants issued in lieu thereof are in circulation. The share-warrants may pass from man to man, and from continent to continent, and no one knows where they are, there being no identity as to the holders. This may be a convenience for an individual living abroad, and for the purposes stated by the Finance Minister, but I do not think it is in the interests of the public, nor do I think it is suited to the conditions in this country. This provision certainly should be withheld from a general Act, until a policy is adopted, whereby our Companies Act has such a general provision. There are a few isolated acts of incorporation containing this provision, and these have been granted only within the last year or two. If it is to be the policy of this Parliament to grant such legislation, then it should be made to apply as well and more particularly to the Companies Act. In this Bill, and in the Bill relating to loan companies, the provision has appeared for the first time as a general provision. I think it, is worthy the consideration of the minister, as to whether this should apply to trust companies and loan companies, when it does not apply generally to companies incorporated under the Companies Act.
The secrecy, the veiled circumstances, seem to be very objectionable in the interest of the public. We grant to a body of individuals certain powers, sometimes large and exceptional, and we know the individuals as they start out; but there may come a time when all knowledge ceases as to the individuality of the shareholders or as to the personnel of the company. For that reason I think this committee should hesitate before stamping its approval upon this proposition. The minister, although he may have considered the matter very carefully, in view of the doubt so generally expressed as to the wisdom of this provision, should hesitate before taking this step at this time, and I think it should certainly be withheld in the case of trust companies and even in the case of loan companies. We have not done it in respect to private corporations in the past.
If we had done so, what harm would it do ?

Because of secrecy. It may not do harm; I cannot put my finger on conditions or circumstances which would demonstrate that harm had resulted, but I think there should be the fullest publicity and opportunity for knowledge with respect to every Act of incorporation granted by this Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I appreciate the view put forward by my hon. friend that there should be general legislation, if it is decided by Parliament that share warrants shall be allowed. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has now under consideration, and will, I believe, within a few days or a week or so, introduce to the House an amendment to the General Companies Act under which permission will be given to issue share warrants. There is no doubt that any change of this kind should be carefully and seriously considered by Parliament, but this legislation is not new. The English Companies Act, under which companies may be incorporated for any of the objects within the legislative jurisdiction of Parliament in England has for a long time authorized the issue of share-warrants.
For trust companies ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would say, yes, with this
qualification, that I have not looked especially at the Act, but I believe that trust companies can be incorporated by the English Companies Act. The legislation is general, and the use of share-warrants is well recognized in England and has been brought about by the demands thalt I have mentioned, namely, from the continental investors. The safeguard is that the shareholders themselves have to pass a by-law authorizing the issue of the share-warrants. I have never known of any case of abuse. One could conceive of a case in which practically all the shares of a company might be represented by share-warrants, but I think iit is hardly probable. As I stated at the outset, I was influenced in introducing this section of the Bill, not by anything that I had especially in mind, but by the fact that trust companies had within the last two or three years sought this power and it had been conferred by this Parliament. As I decided to frame a Bill which would cover any application that might come up for the incorporation of a trust company, it occurred to me that I had better include the powers that had already been granted by

Parliament. My own belief is that the provision as to share-warrants will be inserted not only in the Dominion Companies Act but in the Companies Act of every province of Canada. This will be brought about by the demand of the continental investors for share-warrants.
Would you do it in the case of banks ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would 'hesitate to do it in tlhe ease of hanks, land I do not see the same necessity for it in the case of a trust or loan company as I do ;in the case of an ordinary commercial company whose shares are widely dealt in and in some cases speculated in. Undoubtedly we shall have applications in the way of special Bills brought forward to incorporate trust companies in which this power will foe asked, because the investors will desire to sell their shares on the continent and will be asking for share-warrants. If a Bill such as that were brought forward, in all probability it would pass through the House.

I would hesitate to affirm a positive opinion upon this question, because the matter is altogether new to me. I can understand the advisability of facilitating commerce in shares as in other forms of commodities, because shares are commodities which are sold on the market every day, and there is good reason that we should facilitate transactions in shares. I can see very good reason why this provision should apply to ordinary companies, but as regards banks and trust companies there may be the objection that the character of their shareholders is one of their best assets. The stock of a company is an asset of its creditors. If you can conceive of a bank or a trust company -the whole list of whose shareholders does not appear in its books that fact would be a fatal blow to it because such an institution adds very much to its value and its reputation by 'giving a list of its shareholders to the public. Trust companies are becoming one of the most important forms of management of estates that we have. They are coming more and more to be the managers of the funds of orphans, infants, widows, and so on. The character of the directors is the first asset, and the character of the shareholders is the second; but if you introduce a system whereby it is possible that the whole list of shareholders shall not appear in the books, I doubt if the same security will he felt by the pu >lic in 
regard to trust companies a.s there is at present. That is the only objection that I can see at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does not my right hon.
friend consider that as one reason why the Act would not be abused, namely, because the company would consider the names of the shareholders a valuable asset- and would not permit the occasion to arise under which all the shares, or the greater part of them, would be represented by share-warrants. If we do not insert this provision now, we shall he inserting it in special Bills, so that unless there is some special objection to it, I feel that the provision had better stand.

It is provided in this section that a shareholder cannot qualify as a director by holding share-warrants. A man holding ordinary shares could qualify as director, so that it would not be possible for all the stock to be in the form of share-warrants.

It is my opinion that there is a great deal of objection to the use of share-warrants in ordinary companies. Business is now carried on largely by companies, and the whole purpose of the new Companies Act is to give greater publicity to the affairs of these companies. Snare-warrants are going to defeat that very object; the people are not going to know who are the shareholders of the companies. There is another objection to the use of share-warrants. The local legislature collects succession duties from the estates of deceased persons. By the use of share-warrants a man who wishes to do so may_ defraud the treasury of the province by taking out share-warrants and handing them to members of his family prior to his demise. The object and purpose of our Companies Act should be not to enable companies and corporations to conceal the identity of their shareholders, but to have more publicity; the whole object and purpose of the use of share-warrants is to create secrecy in the transaction of business and secrecy as to the identity of members of companies. While provision for share-warrants is in the English Companies Act, their use is, I understand, not very general in the commercial life of Great Britain, although they are used to some considerable extent on the continent. Legislation of this kind is sought !by rich Brazilian and other companies, so that they may float their bonds

and sell their shares in the old country and at the same time conceal the identity of their shareholders. Personally, I am very much opposed to the use of share-warrants.

There is great force in what the hon. member for North Ontario says. The question is a new one; perhaps the Minister of Finance may think it advisable to leave the matter over for further consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The difference between
scrip certificates of Canadian Pacific railway stock, for instance, and bearer share-warrants, is only a matter of form. My hon. friend might be the holder of twenty-one shares of Canadian Pacific railway stock and if he handed me a stock certificate endorsed in blank I could transfer it to B and it could be passed on to C1 and D and so on until it finally got into some one else's name. The scrip certificate form is used, and I think, will continue to be used, in Canada. I do not know that share-warrants are used in this country at all; 1 am satisfied that they are not used to any considerable extent. The only purpose of this legislation is to meet the requirements of the European market, where they are not familiar with scrip certificates and where they are asking for share-warrants in order more readily to make the transfer of shares. With regard to the succession duties mentioned by the hon. member for North Ontario, it is a question of fact as to whether a decedent was the owner of shares or not and the same consideration would arise in connection with bearer bonds. A, who is the owner of $100,000 worth of bearer bonds, dies. He may have transferred those bonds by delivery to the members of his family or to others; it would be a question of fact as to whether or not he owned those bonds or whether he had parted with them for the purpose of defrauding the treasury of the province. Precisely the same consideration would arise in connection with share-warrants, so that I do not regard that argument as a conclusive one. I repeat that, so far as I know, the only ground upon which the privilege is asked is that of meeting the requirements of the European market. In this country we get most of our money from Great Britain but a great deal of money has been coming over from Belgium and France and the investors in these countries ask 184
for bearer share-warrants. The question is: Shall we make legislation to meet their requirements? If we have not legislation to meet their requirements, they will not so readily invest. The question, then, is whether we are willing to provide facilities under which the continental investor may get the kind of document to which he is accustomed in connection with the holding of shares.

Could not the same object be attained by having a transfer office in London? Provision is made under "the English Companies Act for what they call colonial transfer offices. If an English company wishes to sell its stock in any of the colonies they may establish colonial offices for the transfer of shares. The only argument in favour of the use of share warrants is that they facilitate the sale of stock on the continent. If a Canadian company wishes to transfer or sell their shares in the continental or English markets they could have a transfer office in London or on the continent, which would facilitate the transfer of shares and at the same time remove any objections which might be urged against the use of share-warrants.

I would like to draw
the attention of the committee to the fact that these share-warrants are issued only for fully paid-up stock. Not only would they be a convenience to the people of the continent, tout they would be a great convenience to the trust and loan companies in this country who want to get money from the continent.
On section 51-directors jointly and severally liable:
This is a very important clause. What is the meaning of the word 'knowingly'?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has happened upon a word that was rather carefully considered by the committee; in fact, it was inserted by the committee for the purpose of protecting directors against undue liability. The wording of the section in the Bill as originally introduced, so far as it is relevant to my right hon. friend's question, was as follows:
If the directors of the company declare and pay any dividend when the company is insolvent, or any dividend the payment of which renders the company insolvent, or diminishes the capital stock thereof, they shall be Jointly and severally liable, as well to the company as



to the individual shareholders and creditors thereof, for all the debts of the company then existing, and for all thereafter contracted during their continuance in office respectively: Provided that if any director present when such dividend is declared does forthwith, or if any director then absent does, within twenty-four hours after he becomes aware of such dividend being declared and is able so to do, enter on the minutes of the board of directors his protest against the same, and in either case within eight days thereafter publishes such protest in at least one newspaper published at the place in which the head office of the company is situated, or if there is no newspaper there published, in the newspaper published nearest thereto, such director may thereby, and not otherwise, exonerate himself from such liability.
This was considered by the committee, and I think properly, to be an exceedingly drastic provision. We traced it up and found that it had appeared in Dominion legislation since 1877, but there was no English precedent for it. Our surmise is that it was adopted from American legislation. The committee, after having given the matter very full consideration, came to the conclusion that the section was too severe upon directors. Whether a company is insolvent or whether a payment will make it insolvent, is in each case a question of fact. The result of the section, therefore, would be that, on a strict interpretation, a director who concurred in declaring a dividend when the company was as a matter of fact insolvent, even although not to his knowledge insolvent, or who concurred in paying a dividend payment of which rendered the company insolvent, although it was not to his knowledge that it would do so, would nevertheless be liable under the provisions of this section. The committee, therefore, concluded that it was too drastic, and they amended the section to read as follows:
If the directors of the company declare and pay any dividend which impairs or diminishes the paid-up capital of the company, the directors who knowingly or negligently concur in the declaration or making payable of such dividend whereby the paid-up capital of the company is impaired or diminished shall be jointly and severally liable for the amount of such dividend as a debt due by them to the company.
That is the way it was left by the committee.

I do not think that the amended clause has improved the Bill. In my estimation it has deteriorated it. The Bill as drafted provided that if a director paid a dividend when the company was insolvent, or a dividend which made the company insolvent, he should be liable.
.
For my part I would certainly be in favour of that legislation; in fact, while I cannot speak as to the common law, my impression is that, under the civil law under which I was brought up, without any legislation or statute, the director would be held liable personally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Apart from negligence or knowledge?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My righthon. friend,
I am sure, will agree with me in this: that if the director in that suppositious ease refrained from informing himself on matters that he ought to know about, he would be guilty of negligence. My right bon.

friend -will observe that the sedtion reads, ' the directors who knowingly or negligently concur/ so .that a director who sayts, I did not know, would not necessarily excuse himself from the consequences. If a charge of negligence were brought home to him, ihe would still be liable. While appreciating what my right hon. friend has said, and realizing, I think, precisely what ihe has in mind, namely, that under a clause of this kind it would be difficult to bring home * knowledge ' to a director so as to make him liable, I would like to call his attention to the fact that this section is almost similar in wording to 'section 68 of the Bank Act, which reads as follows:
' The directors who knowingly and wilfully concur in the declaration or making payable of any dividend or bonus whereby the paid-up capital of the bank is impaired, shall he jointly and severally liable for the amount of such dividend or bonus, as a debt due by them to the bank.
For the words 'knowingly and wilfully' we have substituted in this Bill * knowingly or negligently'-making it stronger. For the information of my right hon. friend, I may say that in the Yarmouth case this section of the Bank Act was effectual in enabling the liquidator to recover from the directors of the bank substantial sums paid as dividends in violation of its provisions.

As the hon. minister
knows, when this Bill was before the committee I objected to the word ' knowingly ' on the same ground as my right hon. friend.

Section agreed to.
On section 70-investigation:

I would like to ask the minister if there is any control or inspection over joint stock companies incorporated by the Dominion. For instance, one company is selling Panama bonds in the province of Quebec; another one is advertising guessing competitions in the newspapers and is coining a lot of money.

What is the name of the
Panama company?

The Provident Financial Association, Limited, incorporated by the Dominion Parliament in 1905. Last year I called the attention of the Superintendent of Insurance to the matter, and also that of the Minister of Justice. A circular is circulated in my county and various parts of Quebec, stating that these bonds are guaranteed by the French Government. They are sold to the farmers down there for $52 on the instalment plan, or for $40 cash, 184i
and the farmer also has a chance in a lottery that takes place subsequently. The largest amount he can draw is $96,500.
Is the company incorporated by Parliament?

Yes, it is a Dominion
company, incorporated in 1905. I wrote to the Superintendent of Insurance on March 13, 1913, and he said in reply:
I am in receipt of your xeuer of the 13 th inst. The Provident Financial Association, Limited, was incorporated by an Act of the Parliament of Canada in 1905, but its Act of incorporation does not require it to make a report of its operations to the Minister of Finance. As to the bonds referred to in the circular contained in your letter I have no knowledge whatever. If they are in the nature of a lottery, the parties dealing in them may do prosecuted under the Criminal Code.
There is no disguising the fact that this is a lottery. Large numbers of these Panama bonds were sold in my own constituency to people who did not know any better. They were induced to buy them because on the face of the certificate it appeared that they had been guaranteed by a company incorporated by the Parliament of Canada. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), to whom I referred the matter, wrote to me on April 19, 1913, to this effect:
Ottawa, April 19, 1913.
Dear Sir,-There is not information enough in the papers you send me to enable me to judge as to whether the Panama bonds referred to in the circular you enclosed are a legitimate investment or not, nor would I like to express any opinion upon foreign bonds and debentures. I remember that lotteries were authorized and held in France to raise money for the Panama canal, but whether these bonds are connected with the lotteries or not I do not know. Lotteries are, of course, forbidden under our law.
Tours sincerely,
(Sgd) Chas. J. Doherty.
I have heard no more about it except that I have learned personally that a number of bonds were sold.
During March of this year large advertisements appeared in the newspapers of Montreal and Quebec. The one I have here is in French. It is headed, ' Grand Guessing Competition.' In the centre of the advertisement is a large picture showing a Roman chariot with four horses, and in the chariot a goddess holding a horn of plenty and scattering gold along the way. In the picture are the figures of four women, and the riddle is to make out these figures, which are not apparent at the first glance. This is the inducement offered:

Grand Guessing Contest.
We will give, absolutely gratis, to every person who will find the solution of this guess, one hundred shares in our mining syndicate, formed for the purpose of acquiring and exploiting one of the richest gold mines in the province of Quebec, with the right to participate in ten thousand dollars in gold distributed in prizes amongst members of our syndicate.
Then the conditions follow. The company is the Chesham Gold Mine Promoters, Limited. The advertisement continues:
This $10,000 is to be distributed gratis among the members of our syndicate.

A well known citizen in Montreal, who takes an interest in these matters, and who sent me this information, stated that he was informed on good author-5 p.m. ity that on the first day after this competition was announced on which a reply could be made, the 18th of February, 1,300 five-cent pieces were received, that on the following Tuesday 2,200 five-cent pieces were received, and that on the following Wednesday 4,400 five-cent pieces were received. The whole thing seems to be a sham. The advertisement appeared first in the Montreal papers, and then I saw it in the Quebec papers. The great objection is that this is being done under the Dominion Companies Act. This company was incorporated on the 26th January, 1914, under the Dominion Companies Act. I want to direct the attention of the hon. Postmaster Gereral (Mr. .
Pelletier) to this company. It is called the Chesham Gold Mines Promoters, Limited. The idea of giving 100 shares in a syndicate for five cents! I thought it was my duty to call the attention of the ministers present to what is being done. There is no inspection of these companies, and these things are liable to occur again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) has handed me the statute to which my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) has referred-4-5, Edward VII. By chapter 151 the Provident Financial Association, Limited, was incorporated, but I fail to see anything in the powers granted to them which would enable them to carry on the business which has been described by my hon. friend. The powers set out in the Act are as follows:
The company may

(a)	Underwrite, buy, pledge and otherwise deal in bonds, debentures or obligations of corporations, whether secured by mortgage or otherwise, Dominion, provincial, British, foreign or other public securities, with the privileges and rights thereto attached;
(b)	borrow money upon the security of mortgages, hypothecs, bonds or other securities belonging to the company.
There is no objection that I can see to the legislation of 1905 incorporating hhe company in question. From what my hon. friend has said, I should judge that they are carrying on what is termed a guessing competition. Whether they are violating the provisions of the Criminal Code or not I am unable to say. I think i-t would be impossible to have any return made to the minister which would expose the character of the business carried on by a company having the powers mentioned in this Act. It is quite probable that the powers that were got by the letters patent referred to by my hon. friend are similarly proper in character; but the mode of carrying on business is objectionable. Possibly the Attorney General of Quebec would be the party who might be usefully informed as to the matters brought to our attention by my hon. friend.

I would no-t like there
to be any misapprehension. The sale of the Panama bonds has taken place by a company with a special charter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the company incorporated by chapter 151.

The other company is
incorporated under the General Companies Act. Would any sane man think that he was going to get 100 shares in a gold mine in Quebec for five cents? Yet a lot of people have been taken in-4,400 in one day. There is not the supervision of these matters that there should be. If there is no inspection of these companies iby the Dominion, there should be some prohibition against their misleading the public.

Hon. GEORGE E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):	A comparison of the mileage of the service under consideration with that of the service with South Africa gives the following: distance from St. John to Dunedin, summer service, 15,656 miles; winter service, 15,303 miles. Distance from Montreal to Durban, 8,162 miles; St. John to Durban, 7,802 miles. It will be seen that the distance travelled is twice as great in the service to Australia and New Zealand as it is in the service to South African ports. That of course, makes the expense greater, and the company in charge of the service to Australia asked for an increase in subsidy. I did not grant the amount that was asked, but I did give an increase of $20,000 a year. This service is developing a fairly large amount of traffic. In 1913, $3,364,000 worth of exports of Canadian origin were carried, being about $500,000 of an increase over the preceding year. The increase in the value of exports of United States origin carried was about $270,000, making in all an increase of about $750,000 in the year. The service is being largely used by the export trade of eastern -Canada; the use of the long railroad across the continent is impracticable for most classes of freight. 1 am glad to be able to say to the House that during the last two or

three months the quantity of freight offering for these vessels has been increasing with satisfactory rapidity.

This service was established as an experiment some years ago because manufacturers and others could not conveniently use the Pacific route. We hoped at that time that the service would be well justified by the results, and I am glad to see that so far our anticipations have been fulfilled. Has my horn, friend a list of the freights transported by this service?

I would direct my hon. friend to part 6 of the report of the Trade and Commerce Department, which deals with subsidized steamship services. It has been our aim to obtain a statistical report of all freight carried so that a comparison can be made from year to year and a check kept upon the progress made. The vessels in this service carried last year the following articles of Canadian origin:
Lumber, automobiles and parts thereof, calcium carbide, chair stock, paper, sole leather, agricultural implements, rubbers, iron pipe, hardware, cattle, clothespins, seed, fruit Jars, corsets, cereal food, wire and organs.
Of United States origin the following articles were carried:
Cereal foods, machinery, automobiles and parts thereof, steel rails, organs, lumber, fruit jars, roofing paper, shoe polish, wire and sewing machines.
Of West Indian origin the following articles were carried:
Coffee, cocoa, pimento, ginger and cassava products.
Were there return cargoes ?

We do not have a return voyage. We subsidize the vessels for the trip from Canadian ports for export trade to Australia and New Zealand, but it has been impossible for the company up to the present time to get cargoes which would make it at all economical for them to bring return cargoes to our ports. When they discharge cargo at Australian and New Zealand ports, they load from whatever part of the world they can, generally taking cargo from there to British ports and then returning to our own ports to carry out their export contracts.

My right hon. friend was in Australia last year. Whilst there is no cargo coming back aboard the 
steamers, is there any sign of any future trade from Australia to Canada?

Yes. In another of the publications of the Trade and Commerce Department which details the transactions and exchanges of the different countries my right hon. friend will find set out the articles that return. The traffic between Australia and our own country is now mainly by the Pacific, and it has not been found practicable to get return cargoes to our eastern Canadian ports. But there is a very satisfactory increase in the interchanges between Australia and ourselves. If it would be possible for a provisional arrangement to be made covering certain lines of articles, that would he largely increased. That is shown in the trade between New Zealand and Canada, where we have a mutual preference, the trade, both going and coming, having very largely increased. It is not an extensive trade in one way, yet the increase has been rather remarkable and Canada enjoys a large part of the advantage of that trade, in agricultural machinery, some other kinds of machinery and manufactured articles of various kinds. With New Zealand, which has no very large manufacturing industries itself, our trade in automobiles and motor cars is increasing very rapidly. In paper there has been a very rapid extension of our trade; in fact, we supply practically all the paper for New Zealand, and we are supplying a very large proportion of what is used in Australia so that for our paper industry, our iron industry and the others that I have mentioned there is an extension of trade. Then, there is an opportunity for traffic between Australia and New Zealand and Canada in the matter of fruits, the two seasons being absolutely the opposite of each other. They are taking quite large quantities of our fruit from the British Columbia coast.
From what ports do the ships sail?

From Montreal and St.
John.

What route do they
take?

They take the South
American route by Cape Horn.

Will the opening of
the Panama canal have any effect on the business?
I am not sure that it will make the passage very much shorter, but-one cannot tell what will happen.
Will it have the effect of reducing the subsidy ?
If it makes the passage shorter I am not sure but it would.

Is there not an application before the hon. gentleman for a subsidy when the canal is open for a line of steamers from the east coast to the west coast of Canada, and what consideration does my hon. friend intend to give that matter ?

Several propositions have been placed before the department and the Government for subsidies for lines of steamers connecting the eastern with the western coast by the Panama canal. Up to the present time, although I have given a good deal of attention to the matter, I have not seen that it is necessary to subsidize freight steamers between our eastern ports and our western ports. These are not and cannot be mail carriers; they must be exclusively freight carriers. What may take place when the canal is opened no one knows; but it does seem to me there would be an increase in the lines of steamships from the European countries through the Panama canal to the Pacific ports of Canada, and that it might be quite possible to combine the services between the old countries and those western ports with calls at the eastern ports of Canada. So far as my department is concerned, we are allowing that matter somewhat to develop itself and seeing what the lines and tendencies promise to be before we undertake to subsidize a freight service between ports on these two sides of the country.

Has the minister considered the question of defining a coasting service in view of the opening of the canal ? At present a coasting voyage on the eastern coast of Canada extends from Labrador down to about the mouth of the Amazon, but no farther. There has been an ap-lication from parties connected with the shipping business to have the definition made larger so as to allow coasting vessels to go down to the ports of South America as far as the river Platte. Many of them are getting business that far, and there is no reason, as far as I am aware, why they should not be allowed to go to these southern ports. Then, on the opening of the canal, if we adopt the idea that has prevailed in the United States for many years, we would call it a coasting voyage between the eastern coast of Canada through the canal to the western coast of
Canada. I understand that in the United States a voyage from New York to San Francisco is a coasting voyage, although it is around South America at present, and under that system the business is confined to vessels belonging to the United States. This question of defining a coasting voyage is a matter of a good deal of importance to Canadian shipping, and I was wondering if it had been brought to the minister's attention. It is primarily, I suppose, a matter for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and I have brought it to the attention of the minister of that department during this session. No steps have been taken, but in view of the opening of the canal I think it would be worth while for the Government to consider this question in connection with the coasting trade.

Primarily and naturally I suppose a coasting voyage is that which proceeds'* continuously along the coast of the country to which the ship belongs. The United States, as my hon. friend says, smile at such contractions as that, and their coasting voyages, I believe, go as far as the Phillipines and the widest extension they have. The matter is one that belongs to the Customs Department, I think, more than to any other. I do not think the question of definition of a coasting voyage has come up as a serious matter, but in connection with the opening of the Panama canal it is a question that may very well come up for consideration.
Mail subsidies-Canada, Great Britain ocean and mail service, $1,000,000.

Might I ask the
minister what is being done in that regard?

The present contract expired at the end of the fiscal year, and communications and conferences are now going on with reference to the service for the coming year. I will ask that this item stand for the present until I have full information before the House.

I would like to suggest to the minister that he consider a sliding scale of subsidies for ships according to their speed. As everybody knows, it is very important that we should have a fast service. At the present time the ships participating in this subsidy have different speeds; the Victorian and the Virginian, I understand, are 16-knot boats; the Empresses are about 18 knots, and I think

the Calgarian and Alsatian are even faster than that. Speed costs money and it would be an encouragement fto the owners of ships in this service to get something extra for extra speed. I think it would be a good principle to adopt that when new contracts are made some weight should be given to the speed of the ship, and that more should be paid for a fast ship than for a slower one.

So far as the mail service is concerned, that principle is perfectly legitimate and ought to be acted upon; and it is acted upon to a certain extent. We are trying to get a fleet of Canadian vessels between our ports and the old country which will give us the greatest possible speed. The isbips are being built with satisfactory progress, if not so rapidly as some of us could wish. The Victorian and the Virginian have a nominal speed of 18 knots, but I do not think ithey made that speed from shore to shore. The Alsatian has a speed of I9i knots or more, and the Calgarian is expected to be even a little faster.

What is the speed of
the Empresses?

Eighteemand-a-half knots, and the Royal Edward and the Royal George have a speed of nineteen-and-a-half knots; so that when the Calgarian is in commission our service between here and the old country will run very close to a nineteen-knot service in fairly good weather. That will be an improvement on the old service, and much more satisfactory in a great many ways.
Steam service between Canada and Cuba, $25,000.

Last year's vote has not been expended. The last contract we had was with the Elder-Dempster line, who went out of this service more than a year ago. The question then came up as to whether we should have a subsidized service between our ports and Cuba; and after communications with shipping firms I received the assurance that they would go into the business, preferably, if a subsidy were granted-of keeping up a communication between Canadian and Cuban ports if they were given assurances that they would not be interfered with by subsidized vessels from Halifax and St. John. I agreed, with the proviso that if the service did not prove to be reasonably good I reserved the right to put on a subsidized service. The service (Mr. Sinclair.]
has been carried on by those firms and I think they have fairly met the needs of the two countries. While there is some chance of an export business to Cuba, we have the disadvantage of the preference being given to the United States. Not much is imported into this country from Cuba.

Could not our West
Indian service be combined with that?

No.
Steam serivce between Canada and Newfoundland, $70,000.
Is the service between Halifax and Newfoundland inaluded in that?

No, this is for the service between Port-aux-Basques and Sydney, which is a daily service, Sunday excepted. The two new boats, the Bruce and the Lintrose, have a speed of fifteen and one-half knots and they make the run between Newfoundland and Sydney in about seven and one-half hours. As to traffic returns, I find that this year there have been carried goods of Canadian origin to the value of $981,000 in round figures, and of United States origin $288,232; and that the total value of the traffic shows a slight increase over 1912. The new boats were not in service except for a portion of last year. With the Lintrose taking the place of a less efficient boat the passenger and freight traffic shows signs of increasing.

I had the opportunity of visiting Newfoundland last summer, going via North Sydney to Port-aux-Basques. The new steamer is a splendid boat, and we can congratulate ourselves on Canada's means of communication with the oldest colony to-day. The iservice is very satisfactory. Of course, they have a very strong competitor in the service which is maintained from New York via Halifax, and which carries a tremendous quantity of American goods to Newfoundland. I do not know whether that service receives a subsidy, I would question the wisdom of subsidizing it, as the thing to be attained is the furtherance of Canadian trade, and a subsidy to that service would really be assisting American trade.
It receives no subsidy.

I am glad to hear it.
I thought perhaps the Halifax people, for local purposes, might have asked the minister to subsidize that service. I want to take this opportunity to say to the minister that I do think that the contribution which was announced by the Prime Minister two

weeks ago of $10,000 for the people who have been left homeless in Newfoundland is a very meagre one for the Canadian people to make at this time. Since the date of the announcement of this contribution it appears that the Southern Cross, of whose safety some hopes were entertained, has now, beyond question, gone down with all on board. The situation is that there are a thousand families left absolutely without breadwinners in that colony. I notice that the great city of Toronto gives $5,000, which is one-half of the contribution of the whole Canadian people. I am well aware that in eastern Canada, in the business centres,	which have business
connections with Newfoundland, the personal generosity of the people will be exercised, but we ought to be exceptionally neighbourly to our own kith and kin in this sister colony, and over and above everything else I think the special duty is thrown upon the whole people of Canada of giving such a contribution as will materially assist in alleviating the distress which has arisen on account of this abnormal calamity. I therefore hope that the Government will be more generous and will increase the contribution with a greater sum than that of $10,000 which was announced by the Prime Minister two weeks ago.

My hon. friend must keep in mind that the extent of the disaster, as far as the vessels were concerned, and certainly as far as the loss of life was concerned, was not at all known to the Dominion Government when the cable was sent offering our sympathy and aid. But since then the calamity has widened and more and better information has come to hand. Whilst I am not making any promises, the matter will certainly receive more consideration by the Government. We are closely allied in every way with Newfoundland, and a disaster of that kind is one that appeals to Canada from one end of it to the other.

In reference to freight carriage on the subsidized boats, I would like to know if the minister has any system by which he can qontrol the rates. There is a great deal of feeling along the coast that some of the subsidized boats axe charging too much for freight. The ten-[DOT] dency of subsidizing boats is to drive schooners and other modes of carriage off the routes. On the south coast of Nova Scotia there were a great many schooners carrying freight some years ago, but, as we
began the policy of subsidizing boats between Halifax and the eastern ports, the schooners were cut out of .the business and driven off the routes. The result is that some of these subsidized boats have put the freights up to what is regarded as an abnormal figure along the coast. When these contracts are being renewed it would appear to me to be a suitable time to see whether, if we have not the power under the law to regulate rates, we can do so by contracts. We could arrange with these people to submit their rates to the minister, and he would approve of them before they would be operative. I received a letter a few days ago from people in my own constituency as to the rates which are being charged by the Scotia, which is one of the subsidized boats on the coast of Nova Scotia. The statement made to me was that under the old rate a barrel of flour was carried from Halifax to the small ports on the southern shore for fifteen cents, and that at the present it costs twenty-eight cents. I made some further inquiries, and I was informed that four cents must be added to the fifteen for wharfage, which would make it nineteen cents under the old rate, and the difference is therefore as between nineteen and twenty-eight cents. That is quite a large addition to make, and I have had a number of complaints of that kind. I would like -the minister to say whether he has taken any supervision over the question of rates?

I have taken supervision in two ways. In- the first place, in every one of these contracts there is -a clause, which my hon. friend will find in the latter part of the report to which I referred a moment ago, and which provides that the service shall be performed:
At tariff rates both as to passengers ancl freight which may be from time to time approved by the minister.
The minister has control. None of these vessels can raise the rate which has been approved in a previous year without first getting the assent of the minister thereto. The other way in which the service is being supervised is by having a supervising officer, who travels on all these routes at least once or twice during the season of navigation, makes notes of these things, and calls them to the attention of the minister. In that way we are keeping a pretty fair supervision over these services. I am having the matter to which my hon. friend has called my attention looked into-
Is that provision new?

These last clauses have been added.
