The House resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS.
The House in Committee on Bill No. 130, respecting Certain Patents of Leopold Will-son.-Mr. Fripp. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

Will somebody explain
this Bill?

There are eight patents involved in this. Mr. Willson has been carrying out these patents near Ottawa, and has spent a quarter of a million dollars on them. He now requires a larger plant as well as water-power, and he has interested some Americans, who have acquired waterpower, I think, in the province of Quebec. Only two of the patents have not been manufactured, and the desire is to pi ice them in such position that if any person has manufactured in the meantime he shall be protected. There is nothing unusual in the Bill.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
PATENT OP RUDOLF GOLDSCHMIDT. The House in Committee on Bill No. 135, respecting a certain patent of Rudolf Goldschmidt.-Mr. Fripp. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

The instruction I have received from the solicitor in this case, is, that Dr. Goldschmidt is associated witn Paulsen and Marconi, inventors of wireless telegraphy. Through inadvertence, this patent was allowed to lapse in February last, and he asks to have it renewed, saving the rights of any persons who may have required the right to manufacture in the meantime.

Does a man
with a name like that ever do anything inadvertently?
Hear, hear.

If this Bill is passed, in what position will this man stand as compared with the position he would have stood in had he not allowed the patent to lapse? Is he getting a further extension of time 	.
than he otherwise would have been entitled to?
Yes.

Then I shall have to
register my vote against it.

No injury is done to anybody. He failed to manufacture within two years and by this Bill he is put under the operation of the license clause, which provides that if any person has obtained from the department a license to manufacture he can proceed to do so.

The practice of this House for many years is not to permit Bills of this character to go through, unless the Minister of Agriculture is present to explain them. I believe that it is a very good practice. Bills relating to the renewal of patents ought not be passed in this House without the representative of the Department of Agriculture being present.

The Deputy Minister of
Agriculture was present in the committee and said that this was a proper Bill to pass, and that the department had no objection.

That does not exactly explain the position in which members of this House are before the country. Each mem-k.er.	House of Commons has a responsibility to the people of Canada in regard to the protection not only of public right, but of private right. The fact that a Committee of the House has seen fit to pass upon a question of public and of private right does not relieve each individual member of the House of his responsibility in regard to that. The Government is primarily charged with responsibility for administering the patent law. If the responsible minister will from his place in the House of Commons declare that this Bill is a proper Bill, in which the rights of the individual and of the public are adequately protected-to borrow a phrase from the Premier-then each private member of the House is relieved from responsibility in the matter-he has done his duty by the public; but unless and until either there is an expression of opinion from the Committee of the Whole or from the proper minister, the members of the House are not discharging their responsibility to the people who sent them here. For all I know there may be people in my constituency who elected me for the protection of their interests who may be affected by this [DOT] particular Bill. I have a right to know, on the responsibility of the Government and of the minister, whether that is the case or

not, and I protest very strongly against bills of this class, which necessarily affect intimately private as well as public rights, going through the House without adequate information and an assumption of responsibility by those who are entitled properly to bear that responsibility.

It is something like ten years since I first protested against the railroading of patent bills through this House. I must confess that my protests have not produced very great results, because it seems that the door is getting wider each- year, and it has now reached a stage when a man need not bother whether he follows the law or not; all he has to do is to pay $200 and get his patent renewed. Perhaps the worst offender in the whole 221 of us is my hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp). I do not know why it is; perhaps it is because he is so near the seat of Government that he is chosen as the channel by which these Bills shail be railroaded through. As explained by my hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa, there may be some difference of principle between Bill No. 130 and Bill No. 135. In 1903 Parliament in its wisdom provided that, when a patent is taken out, the patentee can have inserted a provision by which he is exempted from the necessity of manufacturing within two years provided he holds himself ready to lease or sell to another person the right to manufacture the article in Canada. That is done to provide for cases in which there would not be a very large sale, for instance heavy classes of machinery. My recollection of the law is that, either at the time the patent is be>-ing taken out or within six months thereafter, application can be made to the Commissioner of Patents to have this clause inserted. In the case of Bill No. 130, which has just passed the committee after the very lucid explanation given by my hon. friend the senior member for Ottawa, possibly no very great harm is done because it only* allows the holder of the patent to retain his right and he has to give another person the Tight to manufacture. As I understand the explanation of the Bill now under discussion, it is on a different principle altogether. The well known patent law of Canada, of the United States and of most European countries is that the patentee must commence the manufacture of his patented article within two years and continue to manufacture the same so that any one may be able to purchase it; otherwise, his patent is void. A patent is a monopoly given by Parliament to a man who invents a new and useful article. The law of the country says: We protect that man to a certain 'extent; we encourage him to employ his thoughts and ability in seeking out these new devices and we give him a monopoly for a certain number of years providing he complies with certain conditions. This man has been remiss in his duty; he has allowed the matter to drift along and now he comes back to Parliament and says: I was guilty; I was remiss in my duties; I did not fulfil the conditions of the law, but that is nothing. I will pay $200 and you ought to reinstate me in my interest. Supposing I had a note endorsed by a neighbour for $1,000 and on the day of maturity I failed to present that note at the proper place and to send him notice and he said:	' Because you
have failed to do what the lafl demands of you, I will not pay this note,' would not I be laughed to scorn if I came to Parliament and asked to be replaced in my position because I had been negligent? The two cases are. parallel. The way these patent Bills are railroaded through Parliament is trifling with justice and with the rights of the people. It has been stated here a great many times that the granting of patents should be taken out of the hands of Parliament. Why not hand the matter over to the department and let the department in some way exercise a discretion that is a discretion? It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that the Deputy Minister of Agriculture was in the committee. I presume he was there, but the deputy minister knows that this Parliament is railroading these patent Bills through by the dozens. We were guilty when members on this side were in power, and our friends are guilty now that they are in power.

Is there anything to
prevent this man from taking out a new patent?
Well, the law says-
Apart from the law, as a matter of equity?

I can only state what
the law says. He cannot take out a new patent after it has been in force one year. From the equity standpoint, if he sleeps upon hie rights and other men have manufactured his article and purchased it, it is not fair that he get a new patent. I had a very important case in my own practice

some five or six years ago where an American patented a logging engine in the United States and also in Canada. H|s first patent was workable, but he had not manufactured in Canada within the two years. A client of mine spent about $20,000 in building this same machine, not knowing that it was patented. He had gone to the trouble of employing one of the best patent lawyers in Canada, a man having an office in this city to search the record, and he informed my client that there was no patent on that article. The patentee, an American concern, finding that their patent had been infringed upon, brought action in our Chancery Court to prevent my client from continuing the manufacture of the article, and to claim the payment of royalties. It was a long-drawn-out fight, but we won in the end because the patentee had not complied with the law. I cite this instance to my hon. friend to point out that we ought to lay down a definite principle with regard to this matter. Either we should renew these patents or we should not, and if we are going to renew them we should lay down some reasonable rules and hand the matter over to the department to be dealt with according to their discretion.

The hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), is apparently under some misapprehension; the remarks which he has made with regard to the renewal of patents do not apply to these two cases. We are doing no more than what the Patent Act allows us to do: apply to the commissioner, through this Parliament, for the right to renew these patents under section 44, which gives to any third person who applies for license and shows that he has been manufacturing in the meantime the right to occupy the field in the interim. My hon. friend referred to cases where the patentee neglects to renew his patent within the proper time and thus loses his rights. In these cases the rights are still existing, and under the Patent Act we have the right to ask that this Bill be passed. There is a difference between a patent which lapses by non-renewal and one which has not lapsed unless it be by non-manufacture. If the hon. gentleman will look at the Act he will see that we may apply to the commissioner through Parliament for this right at any time, but we have to give within six months to any third person the right to obtain a license or lease from us of our patent rights to manufacture. The argument that Parliament [Mr. Carvell.''
phould not interfere in the case of a patent, which fails by reason of non-renewal and the payment of fees is good, but the cases under consideration come not under that head, but under section 44, which provides-this very remedy.

I am satisfied that my hon. friend is labouring under a misapprehension of the law. The law provides that when a man applies for a patent, or six months thereafter, he may be brought under section 44 of the Act, which provides that the commissioner of patents has the-power to grant to any person the right to manufacture that article by paying a reasonable royalty. If the parties themselves cannot agree upon the amount of the royalty, the commissioner of patents has the right to settle the matter. Under section 38, if the patentee does not manufacture the article within two years his patent is dead. If after the expiration of from six to twelve years a man has not renewed his patent, it expires. My hon. friend himself admits-that we ought not to renew patents under such circumstances, but we are doing it every day. Here is section 38 of the Act:
Every patent shall, unless otherwise ordered by the commissioner as hereinafter provided, be subject, and expressed to be subject, to the following conditions:
Such patent and all the rights and privileges thereby granted shall cease and determine, and the patent shall be null and void at the end of two years from the date thereof, unless the patentee or his legal representatives, within that period or an authorized extension thereof, commence and after such commencement, continuously carry on in Canada, the construction or manufacture of the invention patented, in such manner that any person desiring to use it may obtain it, or cause it to be made for him at a reasonable price, at some manufactory or establishment for making or constructing it in Canada.
That is the provision which has been violated in this case. The man has not manufactured within two years; his patent is dead, yet my hon. friend is asking this Parliament to give back to him that which he lost by his negligence. This is section 44:
On the application of the applicant for a patent previous to the issue thereof, or on the application within six months after the issue of a patent of the patentee or ms legal representatives, the commissioner, having regard to the nature of the invention, may order that such patent, instead of being subject to the condition with respect to the construction and manufacture of the patented invention hereinbefore provided, shall be subject to the following conditions, that is to say:
Any person at any time while the patent continues in force, may apiuy to the commis-

sioner by petition for a license to make, construct, use and sell the patented invention.
That is, while the patent is in force, not after it is dead. The section goes on to
*say:
The existence of one or more licenses shall not be a bar to any order by the commissioner for, or to the granting of a license on any application, under this section, and the patent and all rights and privileges thereby granted shall [DOT]cease and determine, and tfte patent shall be null and void, if the commissioner makes an [DOT]order requiring the owner of the patent to grant any license, and the owner of the patent refuses or neglects to comply with such order within three calendar months next after a copy of it is addressed to him or to his duly authorized agent.
Under this law the patent died because the holder did not manufacture within two years; yet my hon. friend, though he admits that the patent has lapsed through negligence; though he admits that he did not, at the time of application for the patent or within six months afterwards, request that the patent be brought under the conditions of section 44, asks this Parliament to reinstate this man and not only to bring his patent hack to life and to give him six additional years in which to carry on business, but to give him as well the right to come within section 44. This section provides that he need not manufacture in Canada; he can signify his willingness to the Commissioner of Patents to give to another person the right to manufacture in Canada.
Progress reported.

LABRADOR, QUEBEC & SOUTHERN RAILWAY.
The House in Committee on Bill No. 97, to incorporate the All Red Line Railway Company (and recommending that its title be The Labrador, Quebec and Southern Railway Company.)-Mr. Fripp. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-incorporation:
As the member in whose name the Bill stands is here, perhaps he will give the House a lucid explanation of the Bill.

This is a new railway
charter for a line running from some point on the cost of Labrador to the city of Quebec. It was originally the intention of the promoters of the Bill to run across to the Pacific coast, but the committee cut down the charter to between the two points I have mentioned.
As neither the acting Minister of Railways nor the Chairman of the Railway Committee is here, I think the Bill had better stand.
The Rill was very carefully considered in the Railway Committee when both the acting Minister of Railways and the Chairman of the Railway Committee were present.

We have had so
many people seeking railway charters in Canada that when a proposition comes to the House in the way this one originally came-seeking a charter from some harbour in North Labrador which may not be in Canadian territory, but under the jurisdiction of Newfoundland,-and when that proposition has been whittled down by the Railway Committee to a local road from Northern Labrador down to lake St. John, I think under those circumstances we should have a little fuller explanation; especially in view of the fact that propositions of that kind have within them the germ of exploitation, and may not in the end result to the advantage of Canada.

As my hon. friend says, this society originally sought a charter to cross the continent, but at the last meeting of the Railway Committee the Bill was very much curtailed. A large amount of money has already been spent by this company on plans, surveys, etc. The Bill was thoroughly threshed out in the Railway Committee, and it appears to me that the Bill might pass in its present shape.
The Railway Committee gave it a good deal of consideration, and passed it in its amended form.

Why do these gentlemen come here and ask for a line of railway from Labrador to the Pacific coast, and then appear to be satisfied with a line of railway running through absolutely impossible territory, as everybody knows, from Northern Labrador down to lake St. John?
