The House in Committee of Supply.
Steam service or services between Canada and Newfoundland, $7,000.
I understand that there is now a better inspection of these subsidized steamship services by the Department of Trade and Commerce than there has been hitherto.

The inspection of these subsidized steamship services is now a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Until within two years ago, there was really no supervision 9 p.m. of these services at all. We entered into contracts with these different companies, and we exercised as much oversight as we could from the department itself, but we had no system of examination and report in any way. For instance, a claim was made for the opening up of a new route, and that was decided, probably in the minister's office, or somewhere between the club and his office, in conversation, as gentlemen were passing. So far as the conduct of the service was concerned we sometimes got complaints, and then made some examination of these complaints and found out certain things. That seemed to me to be irregular in several ways, so that I appointed a superintendent of these subsidized steamship services, and for the past two years he has been carrying on this work. He has made a yearly trip and inspection of each one of these services on the eastern coast of Canada.
Who is this officer?

Mr. Tupper. If there are applications for new services, he is instructed to go over the routes and report upon the population, the number of towns and villages, the business which would probably offer, and that report gives some guidance to the department, as to whether the application is worth considering and as to how far it ought to be considered. These small services, without supervision, got into slovenly ways; the sanitary conditions were bad; the life-saving apparatus was deficient, the conduct of the vessel during the service was not in point of order what it should be. All these things are taken up by the supervisor, and he reports upon them, and points out the deficiencies, and then the department is in a position to write to these gentlemen and say: you must have such and such put in proper shape. That supervision is jacking up the service, and there has been great improvement. Sometimes vessels are found to be of inferior standard, and notice can be given that a better vessel must be provided or no subsidy will be paid, and in some cases we have got better vessels. Before this inspection was instituted, there was no means of checking up whether a subsidy was greater or less than should be granted, and in order to get at that, there has been embodied in the contract a clause

by which these steamship services are to give thorough statements of their expenses and revenues in reasonable detail. We have then, at least, a basis for a judgment as to whether too large or too small a subsidy is paid. You can then deal more justly with these services, giving those that are worth it a little advance in the subsidy, if that be thought necessary, or, bringing down those which have too much to what is reasonable, but I must say that our subsidies, as a rule, are not placed upon any unreasonable basis. In this way, the different services are, I think, being gradually placed upon a more satisfactory footing.

Has an application been made recently to subsidize a line of steamers between Halifax, Charlottetown, Sydney, and southern Newfoundland? The trade of that portion of Newfoundland is rapidly increasing, but I fear it is going into the hands of the Americans. The trade of Newfoundland last year amounted to over $14,000,000, and we only captured about $4,600,000 of that, while the United States took $5,000,000, and Great Britain $4,000,000. My opinion is that Canada is neglecting the best paying portion of the trade of Newfoundland by not subsidizing steamers to carry it on. There is a very paying trade in the southern part of Newfoundland, and the people there require our manufactured goods, our b'-eadstuffs, and farm products. If a line were subsidized to caitry those manufactured articles to that part of Newfoundland, it would be of great advantage to the people of Canada. The population of Newfoundland is now, I suppose, about
245.000	and is increasing at the rate of
25.000	every ten years. We ought to cater to the trade of that country and to look after it better than we do after the trade of more distant places. It costs less to put our goods on the markets of Newfoundland than to put them on the markets of New Zealand or Australia. We are neglecting places near at hand for places far away. I would as!k the minister to look into the matter and see if the trade between Canada and Newfoundland cannot be increased and if better inducements cannot be held out to our people to deal with Newfoundland. The fishermen of Newfoundland are becoming very prosperous and have money to pay for our goods, and it is the duty of this Government to see that the people of Canada get their fair share of the trade of that colony.
Mr. GEORGE E. FOSTER:	The
trade between Canada 8Dd Newfound-

land, although not of the largest, is still an important trade, os my hon. friend has said. It is also fair to say that the trade services in connection with the Newfoundland trade have been pretty carefully looked after. The trade between Canada and Newfoundland, taking the latest figures that we have, shows a gradual growth. The total imports of merchandise from Newfoundland during the last year were $2,057,297, an. increase of about $250,000 over the preceding year, and the largest in' the history of the trade between Newfoundland and Canada. The exports amounted to $4,472,717, an increase of $350,000 over the preceding year, and the largest by far of any in the history of the trade between the two countries. That makes a total trade of $6,530,014. We have five or six services between Canadian ports and Newfoundland, some of which are of a very superior order. The service between Sydney and Port-aux-Basques is one of the best we have on our coast-good vessels with good speed and so far .as I can learn, well managed. Then, we have a service from Halifax to Great Britain with a regular call at St. John's. We have also a service between Montreal and Newfoundland, with calls at Prince Edward Island ports, allowing of the export of Prince Edward Island goods, as my hon. friend has intimated. Then, we have two other services running out of Halifax which skirt along the southwestern coast of Newfoundland. An application is before the department at the present time for a new service from Halifax via Mulgrave, touching at Prince Edward Island, skirting over to Cape Breton island and thence to Newfoundland. That service is now under consideration, but a decision has not yet been arrived at.
Who are the applicants for that?

The applicants are
Farquhars, the same firm that runs the Seal at the present time. The Seal is a very good boat and is giving a very good service, and that firm is a good firm in the trade service. While it is true that we ought to do everything possible to increase trade- and one means is by subsidized service- there is still a limit, and we have both coasts to cater to and satisfy as far as possible. We have to look a little to the amount of money that it is supposed we can put upon these services. Our trade in the last

two or three years in Newfoundland is gaining in competition with the United States. The latter country has, however, a very good service running as far as Halifax and calling at St. John's, which gives them very direct and very prompt service and we have to compete with that.
Are the reports made by the superintendent, 'Mr. Tupper, available for the members?

Yes, in Part VI of the
reports of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I have seen the
abstracts in the blue book, but the report itself I suppose is much fuller.

The report contains a special report for every service, and it is in a certain way at the service of the House, but these reports have sometimes confidential parts, so that we have to be a little judicious as to whether they shall become public property or not. They are primarily for the information of the department, and then, in so far as they can be made common to the members, for their information. If any member who is interested in any service will come over to the department, I shall be very glad to give him an opportunity of looking at the reports, and in some cases they may be brought to the House.
Perhaps my hon. friend will defer the matter until we come to that item, when I will give him all the information I have in regard to it.

The hon. member for Guys-borough, in dealing with the item before the House, brought up a question of principle that may have a very wide application and may lead to an understanding of a difficulty that has been up for consideration in the House on former occasions. I would like to have the views of the minister with regard to that matter; I refer to the effect upon the rates of the subsidies granted to coastal services. If I understood the hon. member for Guysborough correctly, he offered the suggestion that the paying of subsidies for coastal services had the effect of increasing rather than of reducing the rates. We are facing a condition of increased rates across the ocean. Is there not a possibility that like causes have produced like effects, and that, as a matter of fact, the bonuses or subsidies that we have paid for our cross-Atlantic services are the foundation reason for that condition of monopoly in transportation and continual increase in rates that has taken place during recent years? I need not argue how very important this question is, and how very desirable it is that the House and the country should know where the trouble comes from, if it is possible to find the source of that trouble. The minister has said that in regard to the coastal services he has taken means to inspect, to regulate, and control; but after he has inspected and regulated and controlled, the outstanding fact remains that according to the assertion of the hon. memiber for Guysborough it costs more to carry a barrel of flour between two certain points on the coast of Nova Scotia to-day than it did before subsidies were paid; and it also costs more to carry a barrel of flour or a bushel of wheat from Montreal to Liverpool to-day than it did when subsidies were very much less than they are at the present time. May I suggest, although I am not a maritime man, that just as the subsidy is enabling steamers in coastal services to drive sailing competitors out of the same business, so the subsidy that is



paid to the Atlantic liner enables the liner to drive the tramp from the port of Montreal and then enables the liner to raise its freight rates against Canadian business. The facts in regard to the conditions of the coastal services are established; the facts in regard to the conditions of the cross-Atlantic services are established. As to the reasons for those conditions, if we accept those given by the hon. member for Guysborough in the Case of the coastal service, we are almost compelled to accept the like reasons for the like conditions in regard to the cross-Atlantic service. As a matter of fact the Dominion of Canada is paying immense sums of money year by year to our steamship lines crossing the Atlantic, with the result that instead of our getting a cheaper service we are getting a dearer service. I take the liberty of putting this suggestion before the minister at this stage, whether or not I am in order, because it seems to me that the reasoning is apt, having regard to the assertion of the hon. member for Guysborough and to the fact that the matter is one of such paramount importance to the well-being of this country.

I suppose it is not profitable to devote a little time to the discussion of a question so wide and so important as the one which my hon. friend has just raised, but whether we should attempt that to-night or take occasion to discuss it when there are a greater number of .members in the House is a question of which hon. gentlemen in this committee will have to be the judges. I do not think that anything that has been said by the hon. member for Guysborough has laid a stable foundation for the deduction that my hon. friend has just made: that the rates on our coastal services have been raised because of the subsidies which are being granted. The hon. member for Guysborough mentioned one or two specific cases on one route, which have not at all been examined or looked into. Of course, I am not questioning the information of my hon. friend.

The point I desire to make is that as you pay subsidies to coastal steamers you drive the schooners and the other methods of transportation off the line, and on that account the greatest care is required by the department with a view to seeing that the rates are carefully guarded.

That is a perfectly Legitimate point, but that hardly lays the

foundation for the sweeping conclusion of the hon. member for Edmonton that the coastal service rates are going up because of the payment of subsidies. The hon. member for Guysborough did not go that far.
That is exactly how far he did go.
Then I do not understand him, or he does not understand me.
I think that it is the fact that the tendency of the rates is to go upward, but I do not know of any specific Cases except that of the Scotia, which I have mentioned.

The Scotia is only one out of probably 75 or 100 services, and the case which has been cited with reference to the Scotia has regard only to the cost of transporting a barrel of flour and some other things. What I am trying to maintain is that the assertion of the hon. member for Guysborough is hardly a sufficient basis for the sweeping assertion that the rates of our coastal services are all going up because we are feeding them with subsidies.
Will the hon. minister say they are not going up ?
I think I am quite right in saying that within the last three years there has been very little, if any, increase in prices on our coastal services.
They are subject to your supervision, are they not ?

They are subject to the supervision of the department, and not a single case would occur of allowing them to raise their rates unless it came before the minister himself. I am quite certain that in the two or three years that I have been in charge of this department I have not sanctioned the raising of rates, so far as I can remember, in a single instance. There have been instances in which they have been brought down, but as a general rule the rates in our coastal services for the carriage of products are very reasonable and very low; I do not think that any of our coastal services are making very much money out of the operation of their vessels. With most of them the plea is ,-that they are not making even a reasonable wage for their own supervision, to say nothing of a return on the capital they have invested, and there are few of them who are paying, out of >the subsidies we give and the earnings they make, dividends to their

shareholders. So I think we are on a pretty good basis as far as that is concerned in respect to the coastal service, and I do not *think the hon. member for Edmonton, if he made a full investigation would find that he could base such a deduction as he has drawn to-night. Of course, the old schooner is gone. The hon. member for Guysborough never expects to see her back again in these days of steam and electrical power. There is a place for fihe old schooner, or for the new schooner to be built, or for the sailing vessel, but it is a place which is narrowing every day of the year and every year of our existence. Steam and motor communication takes its place.
With reference to the ocean service, I *think conditions are very different. I do not believe that there is any combine, any conference, any pool in our coastal services; at least if there is I have not come across any symptoms or any points which would lead me to come to that conclusion. But with ocean steamers and those engaged in the world's traffic there is an opportunity for conventions, combines and pools, and there is not a league of the sea in which steamships are not traversing the routes of trade under conventions and arrangements and pools, one with the other, which are carried out the wide world over. One of the most exhaustive examinations that has ever taken place into ocean rates has lately been concluded in the Congress of the United States. I have not been able to read all of the evidence, but I have read the report, and it is instructive to see the outcome of that examination. In the conclusions arrived at by that committee-and a. very able committee I believe it was- they find, speaking generally, that pools, conventions, arrangements, typify the world's seaborne services; that they do exist at the present time; and the committee comes to the conclusion that if they are reasonably carried out they are not only for the benefit of the carriers, but for the benefit of the shippers. The whole thing depends on whether these arrangements are reasonably made and reasonably carried out. In their conclusions they come to these two chief points, first that it is not practicable to prohibit conference arrangements and pooling arrangements and arrangements of different kinds between the different branches of the merchant service of the world. That it is not advisable in the 1851
general interests either of the carrier or the shipper that they should be prohibited; but that what is needed is a system of reasonable control of these services the wide world over, which would be a tremendous undertaking. They have recommended, so far as the United States is concerned, that the control of ocean traffic be taken over by the Interstate Commerce Commission, with enlarged powers and with certain additions to its force of traffic experts as far as seaboard commerce is concerned, and that an attempt be made, which they consider to be the sanest method of approaching and meeting the difficulties, by a system of control of rates. We are to a certain extent confronted with the same problems in our ocean-going commerce between Canadian ports and Great Britain and European ports. A very exhaustive examination was made by a Royal Commission in Great Britain not many years ago on this very thing and the matter has been agitated a lot. I think I explained to the House on one occasion that the British Government and the Canadian Government came to the conclusion to relegate the matter to the dominions royal commission and to authorize them to make an inquiry into these matters of freight rates on produce between Great Britain and Canada and, after having found out the facts, to base their recommendations upon the facts as they found them with a view to establishing a system of control which shall be jointly exercised by Great Britain and Canada so it will have a force and efficacy which it is impossible for Canada for instance to secure herself. The commission have already taken it up in Great Britain and in their trip to Canada they will hold sessions in the various parts of the country and take evidence upon that subject. The shippers will have every facility for putting their case and the carriers will have every facility for putting their case and both will be examined as thoroughly as the commission can do it, in order to arrive, if possible, at the facts in the case. The authority and power of Canada to exercise control over ocean rates is nil, looked at from one point of view, and restricted, looked at from another point of view. We may be told that where we subsidize a line we have authority to a certain extent to control rates. Theoretically we have; practically it is very difficult to do that with reference to ocean carriers. It could be done mucn more effectively if a system of control could be carried out by Great Britain and Canada jointly.

When you come to exercise the small control that you have in view of the subsidy that you give to a few of the carrying lines, you begin to realize how small the power really is to regulate by virtue of these subsidies. Another proposition which has been up before the Government and that has been heard is that the Government shall itself undertake to buy for itself or charter vessels and to carry on a freight service between the ports in Canada and the ports of Great Britain and that they shall cater for the farmer and the shipper of this country and carry freight at cost rates or near cost rates. Any hon. gentleman who thinks of that for a little will see that it is not a light or an easy thing for a Government to undertake. It has been undertaken by governments. In Australia I met with instances of it, particularly with reference to West Australia where it was carried out. In all the evidence I was able to get I could not find that it had been successful in the aim it had or that it had paid the State to undertake the service in the way they did. Perhaps few of us, may be none of us, understand very thoroughly the position of the steamship companies in this regard. My hon. friend from Edmonton said that rates have been raised.
Doubled.

Since the cost of everything has very largely increased in late years, is it not reasonable that rates of carriage by sea should also have been raised? If it costs a ship more for coal, for supplies, and for service than it did, I think it cannot be denied that there should be some remuneration for that increased cost in the way of rates. You may say that the huge vessels of to-day carry very large quantities compared with the quantities carried in former days, but large capacity in a vessel adds immensely to the first cost and to the daily maintenance expenses. If we took one of these first-class vessels plying between Canada and the old country, and inquired into the cost of the ship, the cost of her up-keep, and the revenues derivable from passengers and freights, I think it would probably make us a little more temperate in our statements with reference to the inordinate greed and exorbitant rates of steamship companies. There is the possibility of going too far on the line of reducing freights, and there is need for some system-not yet organized in any country of the world that I know of-which will guarantee reasonable charges for ocean carriage. In a country like Canada where it is

possible by legislation to control freights on all goods carried by land, and where immense sums are invested in transport facilities, the argument is a strong one that if we guard and guide our expensive investments by regulations and control of freights on land, we ought not to lose the benefit of that regulation the moment our goods take the sea to be carried the remainder of their journey on ocean vessels. I think that argument is a perfectly good one, and the only thing is to get some method of deciding what is a reasonable charge. I am not going to pose as an expert on shipping because I am not, but we all know that shipping is more variable than probably any other kind of transport. Transport by railway is comparatively uniform and steady, and it is impossible-although we have gone a great way towards making it-possible

to get, in the course of a few months, a new railroad running over the same course that an older railway has been travelling for years. On the ocean, however, the steamships can go wherever they like; they do not have to lay down tracks for themselves and are not' subject to those stable restrictions that land carriage is subject to. The consequence is that the variations in ocean carriage are immensely greater, are less uniform, and more sudden than they are on land. It was so in the time of the old schooners in New Brunswick. They had their periods of great prosperity, and they sank into periods of equally grei.t depression. They made money at certain times and lost money at other times, and that is one of the difficulties that we meet with when we try to regulate, or even talk of regulating, ocean traffic.

I am sure the committee is under an obligation to the minister for the very full statement he has made, so far as it has gone, but I wish to get at one or two points. First of all, as my hon. friend has appointed a commission to regulate coastal service rates as a condition of payment of subsidy, it seems reasonable that he should do the same in regard to the transatlantic service, in aid of which we are paying very large sums of money. Surely the payment of that money could be made conditional upon some measure of control similar to that exercised over the coastal service, and exercised in somewhat the same manner. In regard to the increased rates in the coastal service as the result of no competition, which, in turn, is the result measureably of the advantage which certain lines have by reason of the

subsidies they have received, I think my hon. friend will agree that regulation of the coastal service rates is an absolute necessity under those conditions. The fact that he has established such a regulation is evidence of its necessity. When these people took advantage of their monopoly of the traffic, which came to them largely because of subsidies, the minister found it necessary to regulate the rates in order that the people should get the benefit of the subsidy they were paying. And so in regard to ocean rates. I say that when we pay a subsidy we ought to have some measure of control over the rates, and I am urging that the minister consider that point in due course and deal with it as may be possible.
Some little time ago there was a discussion in the House, in the course of which it was pointed out that a very large proportion of the grain of western Canada found its route to market by way of Buffalo and New York instead of by way of Montreal. One reason for that was because the rates from New York to Liverpool were less than the rates from Montreal to Liverpool. The reason why the rates from New York to Liverpool were less than the rates from Montreal to Liverpool was because New York was accessible to the tramp steamer and Montreal was not. Conditions at Montreal being as they are, insurance being high and the trade restricted, it is possible for the subsidized Canadian steamship lines to keep the tramp steamers out of Montreal and as a consequence the rates from Montreal are higher than the rates from New York although the distance is less because the tramp steamer gives competition to New York which it does not give to Montreal. The argument is that the condition of higher rates for Canadian freight across the ocean is exaggerated by the amount of money the people of Canada pay in subsidies towards the steamship lines. That is a startling view of the situation. I certainly was startled when I heard my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) make the statement he did but it struck me that it was desirable that the matter should be drawn, to the attention of the House and that we should have the best information the minister can give us in regard to it. There is no doubt about the tremendous disadvantage that the present high rates are to the development of the agricultural industry of western Canada. There is no doubt that it rests as ia
wet blanket upon the development of our country and if it is in any degree the fact that it is the result of the money that we are paying certainly it is a startling condition and one that calls for very close attention on the part of the authorities.

I think the minister will find that these matters are regulated by supply and demand and that it is practically impossible to control these rates. Suppose we did undertake to say what the rates on. 100 pounds of flour, or a standard of lumber, would be from Montreal to Liverpool, the ship would not necessarily come to Montreal. The bulk of the freight business on the ocean is done by tramp vessels, and there is no combine among them, never has been and never can be when they are owned all over the world by various owners who are competing one with another for every freight that is available for carriage. If there are a million bushels of wheat to be carried from Montreal to Liverpool, it is put on the board in London, they all bid against one another, and the ship that will carry the wheat for the lowest rate will get the contract. That is the history of the business. If we should impose a certain rate and say that such and such will be the rate for wheat, or lumber, or any of the exports we send abroad from Montreal to the west coast of England or anywhere else, the result would be that the ships would go somewhere else. Our traffic is only a very small part of the traffic of the ocean. I have on my desk a very interesting little book written by Sir Norman Hill, Secretary of the Liverpool Steamship Owners' Association., relating to the question of the Dominioni's Royal Commission, to which my hon. friend referred, and I have-no doubt that the minister is also familiar more or less with the contents of this book. Sir Norman Hill is an expert upon the question and he gives a great deal of interesting information. One of the things that is pointed out here is that, taking the total tonnage carried by British ships throughout the world, Canada only repaesents 4-7 per cent. All the business that British ships get from Canada is a little over 4 per cent of the carrying trade they do throughout the world. You can therefore see that we	cannot control it	and	that if	we attempt
to put up the rates on lumber or flour or any of these articles and to say that that shall be the rate from Montreal

to Liverpool the ships would 10 p.m. not take it if they could make a penny more by going to the River Plate for wheat, or to any other part of the world, for the whole world is open and a ship may go where she pleases. If she can get a penny a hundred -weight more in the Black sea she will go there. Consequently, if we put the rate lower than the level of what is a good profit from other parts of the world, the ships will not come to Montreal at all, and the consequence will be that we will have to pay more to induce them to come. That will be the result. That has been the result in Australia in connection with the attempt they have made to regulate bills of lading and freight rates. It has been the result in the United States in connection with the Harter Act and it will be the result in Canada if we impose restrictions of that kind. I find from this book that in 1911 the number of British ships engaged in the ocean trade was 4,102 and that of these 1,262 were liners and 2,840 tramps. Out of a total tonnage of 9,853,016 tons, the tramps represented a tonnage of 5,770,000 tons showing that there is a much larger tonnage represented by the tramp vessels than by the liners. The liners which are receiving subsidies from various governments might in some way he controlled, but I am not able to understand bow any single government can control tramps in their trade.
There is just one way, in my mind, of getting our freight rates down and of making them lower and more reasonable and that is by importing more goods. Increase the British preference so as to enable them to get return cargoes from Great Britain to Canada and .in the way the outgoing cargoes will be cheaper. If you will look at the daily reports in the shipping newspapers which are found on the tables in the Library you will see that the most important trade carried on by British ships is the trade between Great Britain and the River Plate. The ships carry out large quantities of coal from Wales, Newcastle, and so on, to the River Plate. The cargo they usually get on the return trip to Great Britain is grain or cattle. Comparing the rates from day to day, you will find that as the rate on grain goes up from the River Plate to Great Britain the rate on coal goes down and as the rate on coal goes up the rate on grain goes down. This means that a ship must have an average rate for her voyage out and back, and that both trips have to be counted to get that average rate. If we in Canada, insist tMr. Sinclair.]
on refusing to import goods from Great Britain, we may expect to pay higher ocean freight rates for our exports to that country. I thought it worth while to contribute this much to the debate, to show the view set forth in this very interesting pamphlet published by Norman Hill.

The question we are now
discussing is of very great interest to the agriculturists of Canada. I have listened with very great interest to the statements made by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), but I fear they have offered no solution for the existing difficulty. The hon. member for Edmonton said that the present condition of high ocean freight rates is a great disadvantage to the agricultural interests of this country, and that we all must admit and cannot dispute. We have also the statement of the hon. member for Guysborough that it is almost impossible to control ocean freight rates, and that if we attempt to control them the vessels will avoid our ports and in that way refuse to carry out produce. This question of ocean freight rates between Canada and Europe is, as we know, from the statement of the minister, under investigation at the present time. As a matter of fact it has been under investigation for a long time past, and we cannot tell how much longer it will take. I point out that the existing condition is of great disadvantage to the farming and other interests of this country, and that it is not likely to be remedied in the near future. If the shipping interests are aware that a question of this kind is to be investigated by a commission, rather than to be dealt with directly by the Government, they are encouraged to put on higher rates, because they know it will take several years before a commission can investigate and report, and, in the meantime, they will enjoy the highest possible rates they can get. If, after a number of years a commission should report that the rates are too high, the companies stand to lose nothing, because, in the interim, they will have reaped the advantage of the high rates. I do not know whether the policy which I would advocate is practical or not, but it does seem to me that the common sense method of dealing with this matter is for the Government to put on a line of Government-owned andi Government-controlled steamers, for the purpose of carrying our agricultural products of Canada to Europe, and such return cargo as can he got. The

existing condition works great disadvantage to our people, and it is a condition that requires prompt and effective treatment. Why, instead of appointing a commission to investigate the matter, which will take years and years to come to any conclusion, do we not deal with it in a way which will check this evil at once. This suggestion is somewhat radical; it is perhaps too radical for this Parliament, but it does seem to me to be the common sense and effective method of dealing with the difficulty. I trust this matter will be given further consideration by the minister; that in the end some scheme of that kind will be adopted, that the shipping interests of the North Atlantic will be given notice that these high rates will not be any longer tolerated, and that the agricultural interests of Canada must be protected against them. I would like to hear from the minister as to what axe the prospects of this Parliament obtaining control over the North Atlantic ocean freight rates. We have American vessels, British vessels, German vessels, Canadian vessels, and it seems to me it would be a complicated matter to organize any tribunal which would have effective control over these various interests.

There is a great fluctuation in these freight rates. For example, about nine months ago you had to pay 60 shillings for cotton from Savannah to Liverpool, but to-day the rate is only 32 shillings for the same freight over the same route. The rates, at present, are extremely low all over the world; they have taken a great drop within the last few months. The trouble about the proposal of my hon. friend (Mr. Steele) is that he would find difficulty in getting work for his ships the whole year around. If he put them into the wheat-carrying trade on the St. Lawrence, I am sure he would not know what to do with them when the season for that trade had closed. If the Government should go into the shipping business they will find they have a bigger contract on hand than any they have undertaken yet. But, of course, all these things are worth considering.

I am afraid that I cannot give my hon. friend (Mr. Steele) a statement which will satisfy him. There are very great difficulties to be met with in any attempt to prohibit, control, or regulate traffic which is world-wide and international. We could do it, of course, in the case of vessels plying between our ports
on the Great Lakes, or coasting vessels, where we would run no risk of any contingency which would inevitably occur when we came to deal with traffic of an international character. Another difficulty would be, that if the Government is going into the business of moving the agricultural products of the country, how could it refuse to go into the business of moving the products which are imported into the country, and which the farmers, amongst others, consume. The importing people of this country are just as strongly against the rates of the steamships as are the exporting people who are sending out the natural products of the country. Both of them, and for the very same reason, want the rates reduced, declaring that they are too high. If you take up those interests, you have to take up the interests of other producers, and the Government immediately goes into a national system of transportation in competition with the wide world. That has its difficulties, one of which has been spoken of by my hon. friend. In matters of other than trivial concerns, our relief takes a great deal of time to- bring about. A email matter can be quickly regulated; you can take it into your own hand; but when it comes to the planets, it takes Providence with all the force of the ages to keep them within their orbits. While those are extreme things to contrast, what I want to bring out is the great difference between managing small and local concerns and managing concerns which run into world-wide interests.
There is always one saving consideration: that is, that competition, whatever we may say, is a .mighty big force notwithstanding all your pools and conferences and everything else. Competition upon the sea is a much easier thing than competition by land, and in sea-borne commerce that competition is constantly exerting itself. Last year there came into the river St. Lawrence some fifty or sixty tramp vessels which took out from that river between 6,000,000 and 9,000,000 bushels of grain. These tramp vessels were in no pool and were competitors of the liners. Do not let us run away with the assumption that the liners are necessarily enemies of tramp steamers. I do not think they are. The liner which comes into Montreal harbour and lies at the dock is a vessel which takes high-class freight and which caters to a very wide area; and bulk products like wheat, she takes only as a last resort. If she cannot fill up with other freight, she will take wheat; and if she haa a hold big enough for a thousand bushel*

of wheat she will take the wheat. If she cannot get 5 cents for it, she will take 2 cents; and if she cannot get 2 cents she will take li cents, or anything that will pay for the cost. You could not possibly make a head against all those forces by a Government system of carriage, which would have politically and economically to widen itself to all the demands of all the producers and of all the consumers in this country. The tramp steamers would still exist; our Government vessels would not drive them off the face of the ocean; they would come and take the wheat, as they did out of Montreal last year, and would leave our Government steamers there. Of course, there is the ready answer to this that the Government would be able to stand the loss, supposing they made one. But the Government, after all, is all the people aggregated, and every man has to pay his shot into the locker.

Has the minister made any progress in regard to the insurance rates on the St. Lawrence? The high rates are one reason why the tramp steamers are kept away from the St. Lawrence. Some intimation was given that the Government was looking into the matter, and I would like to know if the minister has had any success in lowering the rates.

We Canadians are optimistic and we rightly stand toy the statement that we are the best country in the world and can do almost anything; but we are still subject to atmospheric storms and geographical conditions. No matter what advantages we have, we have some disadvantages, amongst which is our geographical position, and the question of insurance plays a great part in that respect with reference to our freight. Whether rightly or wrongly, insurance rates are higher for the St. Lawrence and for ports along a certain range of north Atlantic territory than they are for those that lie to the south. We may think that this is not right, that it is unjust. We may say:	Look at our
buoys, our lights, at the immense sums we have expended; see how we have made almost a lighted street Of the St. Lawrence until you get out past the	Strait of Belle Isle.
Yet when you go to the hard-headed men of business who manage the marine insurance of the world, and talk to them, they simply meet you with the statement: It is all a matter of demand and supply,

and the rates are higher there because in the working out of the insurance business it has been demonstrated to us that we must have higher rates or else make greater losses. My hon. friend has said that some intimation was given that the Government was looking into the matter. So they were; and I think I made the statement myself that if the men who are interested in the Dominion of Canada will organize themselves into a combination and put their capital behind it in order to bring about a system of insurance which will make it easier for vessels, tramp and others, to come into the St. Lawrence and what you may call the interdicted ports, so far as higher charges are concerned on the Atlantic, the Government is sympathetic to a movement of that kind and will help it. That challenge has been made; but the shipping interests have not taken advantage of it; they have not organized themselves. If they would do so and would put themselves behind an organization to help to make matters better, the Government would be quite willing to assist them materially in doing it; but the Government is hardly in a position to ask the people to take the matter of insurance into their own hands for that part of the Atlantic, and to bear the risks and burdens and what is also a very great item, the conduct and management. There again is an item which bulks laTge when any demand is made that we undertake a Canadian system for carrying the freight of this country that is to be managed on business principles. It is a very difficult thing for a Government; and I, for my part, feel that the matter should be very gravely considered before the Government of Canada should undertake to do the ocean-carrying business of the Dominion of Canada.

Representing a large number of farmers who have often expressed their opinion to me on these matters, I feel it my duty to say that this difficulty which is presented in various forms, whilst being undeniable, is not insurmountable. The hon. minister has just outlined the fact that the problem before him is difficult and the Government hesitates to undertake to solve it, but that does not excuse the Government. Great Governments will do great things. If this country were at war, they would take possession of all the means of transport, guard all the avenues of output and of import and see to everything. Napoleon once held Europe in the palm of his hand. He

blockaded the whole continent of Europe at one time.

Yes, and Europe had a
hard time of it for many years.

Yes, because he was in supreme control; that only emphasizes the point I am trying to make. Surely in this age we are not going to throw up our hands and say, because a difficulty is a great one, that it is therefore insoluble. The very fact that some system of national insurance could be contrived, if the different interests of the country would bind themselves together for that purpose, shows conclusively and at a glance that it is the Government's duty, as representing the people, to undertake that very thing. That is the function of government. People combine in communities and in nations for the purpose of having combined interests and of managing them in a combined or national way. Governments, I submit, are elected for that purpose and accordingly as they display capacity for administration, so do they make for the success of the national interests, as well as of the individual. If the farmers must be told that their produce will have to run the chances of an inclement clime, of rivers difficult of navigation and of all the other troubles that arise in a country like this; if that is the final finding of this Government, why then we must accept it. If it is a correct finding, we must resign ourselves to our fate, but the simple fact that the problem is a difficult one is surely no excuse for leaving it unsolved.
Change the Government.

That would only make it worse. We surely may expect that such a minister as we have will grapple with great things and solve them. We have tremendous means of internal transportation, but we are blocked by the sea. For my part, I have been thinking this question over for many years; I have been reading it up to the best of my ability and associating myself with those who understand it, and I must confess that I do not understand it, notwithstanding the fact that I have brought myself in contact with those whose interests are most involved. I cannot help saying however that I view with great disappointment any statement to the effect that another year is about to close without some supreme effort being made to solve this question. It is all very well having commissions of various kinds who bring in ineffectual findings, which are pigeonholed and that is the end of it; we farmers want to see these things grappled with; we want to see them solved. Speaking in a somewhat radical way, I think that if a government at any time finds that it cannot do things, it is that government's duty to give place to another. I am speaking in a gen-ral way; I .do not know that anybody in this country would for one moment advise such an exchange of horses as was suggested a moment ago. But it is a well-known maxim of law and equity that there is no wrong without a remedy. It is certainly no sign of strength, no sign of progress, no sign of aptitude that year after year we cannot do what other countries can do. Look at little Holland, covered with the sea, as it was. She shut the sea out; she actually defied the sea by raising dykes and pumping them out. Holland is a country of marvellous prosperity; she has become a country of happy and prosperous people. Now here are we with enormous natural resources, as we are told every day, and with great wealth; yet, in confusion, we are actually throwing up our hands before one of the most ordinary difficulties of everyday life. The farmers ought to feel that those in charge are capable and are ready and willing to do their duty in this respect. The farmers must know that the Government have some plan or will mature some plan which will give the farmers better facilities for the carrying of their produce and the transaction of their business. The farmers, as we all know, not being banded together in well-connected relationship like other classes of business men are unable to grapple with these ques-^ tions for themselves; therefore they must be particularly looked after by the Government. Other branches of business can by instantaneous communication or by well-conducted methods of business contrive plans for the solution of their problems. The farmer is, of course, an authority on the question of [DOT] the productions of the soil; he is not an authority on business by any means. I cannot emphasize it too strongly that the wish, nay, the demand of the farmer is that the present or some Government will rise up in Canada and solve the question of ocean transportation; and it must be solved.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that was before the department first in the year

1901, on different occasions between that year and 1908, and again in the form of a petition during the last year. I refer to the efforts that the people of Mira River have been making to get a subsidy for the steamship which runs up that river. When the matter was brought to the attention of the hon. minister's predecessor, I think he took the ground, that the Government was not supposed to grant subsidies or subventions to boats running upon inland rivers. The late Government voted sums of money to build public wharfs up that river, and this Government carried out the intention of the late Administration by building those wharfs. I think that does away with the objection that the Dominion Government should not subsidize vessels running upon inland waters like the Mira river. A large petition has been placed, I understand, with the minister or in his department by the residents of Mira, and I simply want to support the claims of those people as best I may. The Mira river is being navigated by a steamer which carries passengers and freight for a distance of between 25 and 30 miles inland. At the entrance of the harbour there is a Tailway which connects Louisburg with Sydney, and the river is the only means of transportation by which the farmers along the Mira-and it is a fine and thickly-settled farming district-can send out their produce, unless they drive between sixteen and eighteen miles either to Sydney or to the mining centres.
1 take the opportunity of bringing this to the attention of the minister to see if it is not possible to include in his supple-mentaries of this year some appropriation for this purpose. The Government have undertaken to build wharfs on that river.
I think the Government should help the residents of that section of the country farther by granting a small subsidy to this river boat. The local Government grants a subsidy to the boat, but it is rather small and they are looking for a daily service. Any person undertaking this service, even a subsidy, would have to be very wide awake to make a daily service pay.
I will look into it.

We are on item 162, the service between Canada and Newfoundl-land. I have often thought, and this is my excuse for saying a word or two at this late hour, that there are great possibilities of trade between Canada and New-
foundland that are not taken advantage of to the extent that they should be. The people down there trade very largely with this Dominion. The hon. member from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean) gave the figures, so I need not go into them. I speak as a casual visitor having visited the island last summer. I was very much struck with the number of Canadian goods displayed, and in conversation with men of commercial standing there I discovered that our own people appear in their minds to be backward about catering for the tirade. I notice that the people down there are practically Canadianized. I think that the banks of Nova Scotia, Montreal and Commerce give them their currency. Canadian money passes current there from hand to hand and they speak absolutely our language with a delightful addition to it of the Irish brogue. They say it is the land of fish, frogs, dogs and Irishmen. I found a quiet desire for a closer trade relationship and I believe they are really anxious to have closer relations; and yet for some reason, for something that happened in the past which I need not go into, there is a reticence about entering into any closer alliance with us, national or commercial. Cabot's Head is the gateway of Newfoundland. At that point you enter through rugged cliffs on each side, into a most beautiful harbour, the crowning cliffs showing impregnable strength. I could not but be impressed that Newfoundland was not only the gateway to Canada but the gateway to British North America and to North America and I felt that if something could be done, whether along trade lines or otherwise, to round out the Confederation by bringing in that splendid colony, people of kith and kin to ourselves, it would be a great step in advance. There is along the southern coast of Newfoundland splendid territory for hundreds of miles from Port-aux-Basques to Placentia bay and then to St. John's. Every village along that coast is remote from the (railway, it is essentially a place for ocean trade; and with the progress that Canada has made there to-day, with the cordiality of feeling which I heard expressed by prominent business men and others, I think the time opportune to press for some measure to increase our trade with Newfoundland. During the fifteen years that hon. gentlemen opposite were on the Treasury Benches nothing was done in that direction. I think we on this side of the House might bring

to the attention of the Government the great possibilities of increasing trade there. I found a peculiar thing down there. The people of that colony are adventurous traders. I saw boats loaded at St. John's with codfish for South America. I found that they shipped also to the European countries. I found that the supply of fish was almost inexhaustible and while their trade is growing largely away from Canada and while they leave our Maritime provinces to supply us as they can with fish as far inland as refrigerator car service and other railway equipment will be able to carry it, the trade of Newfoundland in natural products, which I understand are largely fish and pulp and some minerals outside of the Belle Isle mines, has yet to be exploited and developed. Their trade is now moving in other directions and we should make an effort to secure a larger proportion of that trade, especially when they are so willing and anxious to receive the produce of this country. When I saw the moderate sum of $70,000, in that Estimate I was surprised; my idea rather runs to $700,000. I have no accurate data but I wish to convey my impression of the possibilities that exist there. Whereas to-day our export trade to Newfoundland amounts to $4,000,000 I think with a little extra pushing we might easily increase that to ten or twelve millions dollars to the great gain of the producers of Canada,

I wish to take issue with my bon. friend's statement that the late Government did nothing to increase trade with the colony of Newfoundland. The British preference stimulated trade between Canada and Newfoundland to a very large extent, and I (have no doubt that the preference is largely responsible for the increasing trade between those two countries. That is to the credit of the late Government who extended the British preference to all British colonies. The present Government, although it bias been in power over two years, has nothing to its credit in the way of increased trade with Newfoundland. My hon. friend was the first to introduce politics into this discussion, and I did not want to let the opportunity pass without giving him a little light on the question as to which party is entitled to the credit for the increased trade with Newfoundland. There is a way of increasing that trade still farther. If my hon. friend will persuade the Government to give an additional preference to that colony, he will find that Newfoundland will respond, and I am sure that that would do more towards increasing trade than paying subsidies to steamship companies.
Steam service between Halifax, St. John's and Liverpool, $20,000.

What company gets that?
Mr. FOSTER- Furness, Withy and Company.

Has the minister the
rate- schedule of that company?
Do they submit rates each year when the contract is renewed?
They raise the rates, they do.
Are the rates the same this year as last?

Just the same.
Steam service between Montreal, Quebec and Manchester, England, $35,000.
What company gets that?
The Manchester Liners, Limited.
Do they carry the mails?
No.
What is the object in subsidizing that line?

For the extension of our traffic. As my hon. friend knows, Manchester lies in the centre of the most populous district in Great Britain, and I would like to call the attention of my hon. friend to the increases that have taken place in that connection. This service carries a large amount of freight. Last year it took a total tonnage of 269,438 in weight and 72,761 by measurement, as compared, let us say, with 1908, when only 112,759 of weight was taken. The trade has more than doubled, and is constantly increasing.
It is simply competing with the tramp steamers.

If the tramp steamers are there, they will compete. As to the value, $8,246,791 worth of goods of Canadian origin were carried, and $3,000,000 worth of goods of United States origin; that is, they carried over $12,000,000 worth of

freight, which represents an enormous amount of stuff. The subsidy is not a large one.
Mr, SINCLAIR: In that case they ought to be able to run without a subsidy.

There is that question as to whether or not, and to what extent, these services ought to be self-supporting. One object I had in view in demanding a statement of revenue and expenses, was that with data covering a period of two or three years one might be able to judge as to whether this or that line ought not to be allowed to go on its own resources.
Steam service between St. John, Dublin and Belfast, $7,500.
Who gets the Irish subsidy?	_.
The contract is with the Ulster Steamship Company, Limited. Last year they carried goods of Canadian origin to the value of $1,200,000.
How much of that was deals?

There were some, but
they also carried wheat, barley, rye, lumber, flour, oats, apples, hay, linseed cakes, washboards, steels, and handles. They carried a large amount of general freight.
Winter steam service between St. John, Halifax and London, $15,000.

The Canadian Pacific
railway has that contract. Last year they carried goods of Canadian origin to the value of $2,600,000, and $1,141,000 worth of goods of United States origin-a total of nearly $4,000,000 worth.

How many trips do
they make?
Ten.

What is the object in
paying that subsidy?
The purpose is to stimulate trade between the two countries.

It seems absurd that
we should have to subsidize freight steamers for carrying goods from St. John and Halifax to London, when there are a dozen companies willing to carry the freight at ordinary rates. We are not trying to develop trade with London especially, are we? If we are not getting any reduction in rates toy paying this $15,000, what are we paying it for? That is the point that wor-

ries me. If it were a particular trade that was being developed, if these vessels were carrying apples from Annapolis, for instance, it would be a different matter; but if this company is simply carrying deals or ordinary freight we are throwing away our money.

It is not quite fair to say ' if they are only carrying deals ' because they are not simply carrying deals. Let me direct my hon. friend's attention to the situation. These services were not started last year or the year before. They had been subsidized for a series of years, going back to twenty-five or thirty years ago. The very same question that was asked to-night might have been asked, and it might have been just as difficult for me to answer it as it has been to-night, at any one of these times. There was really no data before the department until we undertook the system of trying to get at just about what were the revenue and expenses of these different lines. We could not do that in one year, but taking it over a period of two, three or four years, you have the data for making up your mind and basing your judgment as to whether this particular line, or any other, ought to be assisted. I think we must come to the time when our freight services between large cities or countries must carry their own charges and costs, and we will gradually become limited in making provision by way of subsidy to services for the carrying of the mails with as great speed as is required and to pioneer services breaking the way into new countries where we have great difficulties to encounter in carrying and establishing trade. In the course of time I hope we will be able to do some work of discrimination with respect to these services, which I have found impossible because I had no data.
Steam service between Canada and Australia or New Zealand, or both, on the Pacific ocean, $180,509.
Are our imports from Australia increasing ?

Our exports and imports both are increasing. In 1913 the value carried out of Canadian origin was $770,412, and there was a large amount of United States origin, the whole value being between $3,000,000 and $3,500,000. It would be more satisfactory if the returns of the department were looked at to see the different lines into which this trade was divided.
What do we get from them particularly ?

Exports of Canadian products increased from 52,574,000 11 p.m. in 1902 to 53,954,000 last year.
There were foreign products to a small amount, making the total exports about 54,000,000. The imports are much smaller, amounting to a

 little less than $500,000. In the trade exchange between us and Australia, the balance is very largely in our favour; Australia raising much the same character of staple products as we do ourselves.
Do we send any agricultural implements out there P
Some agricultural implements go there, and they are very well thought of, too.
I suppose the subsidy decreases as the business increases ?
The subsidy, as are all our subsidies, is a stated sum during the term of the contract.

The hon. minister says that there is a very large increase in the business. It struck me that there might be a corresponding decrease in the subsidy, because the increased business must give a much larger revenue to the steamer.

Yes, on a strictly logical basis that would be so, but our subsidies vary a little from that basis.
Steamship service between Victoria and San Francisco, $3,000.
Has any progress been made in regard to the application on behalf of some interests in the town of Yarmouth and vicinity to subsidize a steamship service between Yarmouth and Boston ?

Yes, so much progress has been made that I have been obliged to decline paying any subsidy to the line of steamers that run between Yarmouth and Boston. The Yarmouth line of steamers were on the point of increasing their service and then an attempt was made to get a subsidy from the Dominion Government. -On looking the whole matter over, and upon considering it, I was obliged to say that I believed they ought to carry their own costs and charges and improve the service. They have improved the service since without a subsidy.
Has there been any proposal made to subsidize a new line of steamers between Shelburne and Boston?

I do not know whether you could say that a proposal has been made or not. There have been communications and a deputation visited Ottawa and talked over the matter with me. But aside from the general idea that they would like to have a service between Boston and Shelburne, there was no founded proposal upon which a judgment could be taken as to the subsidizing of a service. Generally speaking, we have not subsidized direct services between our large cities and the large American cities. Although the matter has not been absolutely decided upon, I still think there will be difficulties that cannot at present be overcome in endeavouring to inaugurate a new and up to date transport passenger and freight service between Boston and the ports on the southern coast of Nova Scotia.

A condition of affairs has arisen in respect to the trade between Nova Scotia and the New England states particularly in regard to the transport of fish that has not hitherto prevailed. The United States markets are free to the fishermen of Nova Scotia. The fishermen of the west-tern part of Nova Scotia would appear to be pretty well served by the very excellent steam service which has been established for so many years between Yarmouth and Boston. However, the fishermen in the eastern portion of Nova Scotia are not so well provided with means of transportation in that respect. There .has been a very excellent line of steamers established between Charlottetown, Port Hawkesbury, Halifax and Boston. Unfortunately, however, there are other very important centres of the fishing industries lying along the coast of Nova Scotia which are not served by any direct communication with Boston and I would like the minister to have an open mind in regard to the propriety of subsidizing some service between Nova Scotia and Boston and giving it the same consideration that he gives to other services that are bonused for the purpose of promoting traffic and the interchange of commodities between different sections of the British colonies.
There are very important fishing centres at Arichat and Canso, where are caught large quantities of fish, which will naturally find a market in the United States. At present, there is no means of ready transport, by reason of the fact that the steamers do not call at any intervening port between Port Hawkesbury and Halifax. It would be worth while for the minister to consider

whether he could not give a subsidy to the Plant Steamship Company, in consideration of their steamships calling at Arichat and Canso, for the purpose of taking fish shipments, which would find a much more profitable and ready market in the United States than they can find within our own territory.

I would like to urge the same point on the minister, as it is a matter that my constituents are deeply interested in. I took occasion some time ago to bring the matter to the notice of the Minister of Marine, and we had a discussion on it, and a number of reasons were put forward by gentlemen on this side of the House in favour of granting some assistance to a line of fish boats to ply between the south shore of Nova Scotia and the Boston market. It is obvious that we should be able to take advantage of the free open market of the United States, but we cannot do' so with our present transportation facilities. The town of Yarmouth has transportation factilities to a certain extent; I understand there is a boat from Yarmouth to Boston making three trips a week.
Four.

The Yarmouth people
are able to forward their fresh fish to the Boston market, and I am informed, on the best authority, that the result has been that the price at Yarmouth has about doubled since the United States duty on fish has been removed. Fish is a very perishable commodity, and unless it is put into the market quickly it is almost impossible to carry on a trade in it at all. At Canso, we have had a dead slow price of $1.50 per hundred pounds for fresh haddock and fresh cod, for a number of years past, while at Yarmouth they have been getting on an average during the present winter $3.86 per hundred pounds for the same kind of fish. The Montreal market is a good market as far as it goes, but it is expensive for us to send to Montreal, and the freight by water, from the ports of southern Nova Scotia to Boston, would be very much less than we could possibly expect them to be by rail to Montreal. Then, Montreal is a small market, and if you put more than two or three carloads of fish into it in one day, you break the market. On the other hand, you can bring as much fish as you like to the Boston market, because it is a great distributing point for Chicago, New York, [Mr. Kyte.f
and the big cities of the United States. The price at Boston goes up and down, but sometimes it is quite high. Sometimes it is lower than in Montreal, but the average Boston p-ice is much better than the average Montreal price. We can never expect to get a large fish trade developed on the south coast of Nova Scotia, with our present home markets. The United States market is now open to us, and the one thing needed to make a great and profitable business for the people of Nova Scotia, is transportation facilities. The Minister of Finance told us that our trade with the United States is large, because we purchase from the United States in great quantities, but here is an opportunity to sell them a commodity that we have on the southern shore of Nova Scotia, and for which a ready market is waiting in the United States. I have no doubt that if we had those facilities our fish trade with the United States could be worked up to be an enormous industry. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will find that during the past year enormous strides have been made in the fresh fish business in the town of Yarmouth, because of the Wilson tariff. We can equally develop the trade at Canso, Isaac's Harbour, Drumhead, and a number of other places along the coast of Nova Scotia. I would suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should get collecting boats to take the fish to some particular point, from which there would be a subsidized line to take it to the Boston market. I do not know what the difficulties are, but I cannot conceive that there should be any difficulties which would prevent that being done. I hope the minister will have an open mind on the question, and that he will carefully look into it, because I think it is one of the opportunities which our people in Nova Scotia have been looking to for a long time.

I quite understandthough not so well as my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) who lives in the atmosphere- the possibilities of the fish trade of the Maritime provinces, particularly of that most highly endowed province of Nova Scotia, in that respect.

In every respect.
Mr, FOSTER: At the same time, there are difficulties in the way of having a fast line of steamers running to Boston, from all the eligible points in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, for developing the trade in fish. A very large

amount of money could easily be spent in arranging fast services at frequent intervals, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) will see that there would be difficulties in multiplying steamship services from all these eligible points. The fish trade of Nova Scotia is flourishing; it gives very large employment; it has a large number of men, who are not men of capital, to gather the fish, but it has also a large number of men who are men of capital, and who are able to put their means into the services necessary to transport the fish to the markets awaiting it. From Halifax and from Yarmouth you have direct lines of steamers running to this market. From Yarmouth you have another eligible line of steamers, and the line that runs out of Yarmouth does not simply serve the harbour, but the coast next to Yarmouth. Yarmouth is a centre for collecting from tihe south of Nova Scotia and even from points as far distant as Mulgrave, by the railway communication which they have and which caters very largely to the steamship companies that run out of Yarmouth. It would be a good thing if we could get in all these boats, but there are some difficulties in the way. It is a common idea amongst some that we are made of money and $100,000,000, or any number of million dollars should not stand in the way. We must be careful in one way to keep some cheek on our administrative expenditure; we must on the other hand 'have an open mind and look into these questions as thoroughly as possible, which I am well disposed to do with reference to Nova Scotia, because I know the value and the increasing value of its industries. Possibly a (little time and patience will do a great deal for uts in that respect.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1914, between Gaspg basin and Dalhousie or Campbellton, $20,000.
Will the minister give us some information about that?

We had that service under contract with the steamer Canada for a period of years at a subsidy of $20,000 a year. That subsidy was made up of an advance of some $5,000, just a year or a year and a 'half ago. That grant was given because that portion of the coast showed a growing trade. There is in the first place, as my hon. friend knows, the competition of a line of railway which runs along the coast which does not serve all the points or the ports. In consideration, however, of local considerations, $5,000 was added to
the subsidy a year or so ago, and a contract was entered into with the Canada, a very good vessel, so far as I remember; but the proprietor of the Canada died and his estate was not able to carry on the service. Therefore we have arranged on very short notice, because all this has taken place within a short time, to carry on just about half the service at half the sud-sidy, using the Canada as one of the vessels and the Gaspesia, a vessel which will be known to my hon. friend, to carry on the other part of the service. We subsidized just to the same extent in point of distance and to the same ports, or very nearly so as were served under the old steamship contract with the Canada, but the service is distributed between the two vessels.
